title: Reduce, reuse, recycle: why a peel rots and plastic stays
playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if done at home today, in a city flat, with the materials listed. The rot jar test gives each thing its own clear jar, pressed against the glass, so a child sees changes without digging. It uses soil from a pot where a plant has been growing for some months, or two handfuls from under a tree outside, because new packaged potting mix and cocopeat hold few microbes. The plastic is a strip of an empty milk packet, which every home has, instead of a thin carry bag. The cloth must be pure cotton, because polyester is a plastic. The soil must be damp like a squeezed sponge, not soggy, or the jar smells. The peel shows big changes within a week in warm months. In a cold winter, run the test for three to four weeks indoors. Cotton and paper change only a little in two weeks, which is a real result, so the table scores 'how much is left' from 5 to 0 instead of 'rotted or not'. The crayon test works only with wax crayons, and is heated in a bowl over hot water by a grown-up, never on a flame. The bag test uses 1-kilogram weights that most kitchens have (full 1-litre water bottles, or sealed 1 kg packets of atta, rice or dal), stops at 10 kilograms, and has a grown-up lift once a bag holds more than 3 kilograms. A thin plastic bag is often stronger than children expect, and the unit treats that honestly. The newspaper bag's bottom fold is hard, so a simpler fold is given. The T-shirt bag needs a grown-up for the thick cuts. Recycled paper needs 1 to 3 days to dry, and works without a mixer by hand-mashing. Both games were played through with two and with four players, and every card and square does something. The newspaper bag needs 30 minutes to dry with paste. Start the rot jar test on day 1, because it runs for two weeks.

summary.text: A banana peel left on soil is gone in a few weeks. A plastic packet left in the same place is still there years later. The peel rots because soil microbes feed on it, using enzymes that fit its molecules. Almost no microbe has an enzyme that fits plastic yet. So the best plan is to make less waste in the first place. Next comes using things again and mending them, and recycling comes last. You will bury four things in jars of soil, act out a bottle's journey, and mend something at home.
summary.art: A child holding an empty plastic bottle, with a dotted path behind it winding past a kabadiwala's cart, a sorting shed, a factory and a T-shirt, and a second path going to a smoking dump. Above, a clear glass jar of soil with a blackened banana peel and an unchanged strip of milk packet pressed against the glass.

intro.hook: Hold a banana peel in one hand and an empty milk packet in the other. If you buried both in a pot of soil today, which one would still be there when you are grown up?
intro.text: Every day, Indian homes throw out peels, packets, bottles and paper. A van or a cart takes them, and we never see them again. But they have not left the world. They have only moved somewhere else. A banana peel can turn into soil in a few weeks. A plastic toothbrush made when your grandparents were young may still be lying somewhere today. Why does one disappear and the other stay? The rot jar test will show you, and the science will explain it.
intro.art: A child at a doorstep holding up a banana peel and an empty milk packet side by side, a garbage cart disappearing round the corner of an Indian lane, and a question mark floating above the cart.

outcomes: I can say what reduce, reuse, repair and recycle mean, and why reducing comes first.
I can run a fair test to find out which things rot in soil and which do not, and record what I see over two weeks.
I can explain that peels and paper rot because microbes cut their molecules apart with enzymes, and that most plastic does not rot because almost no microbe has an enzyme that fits plastic.
I can describe where waste goes in an Indian city: the dump, the compost yard, the waste picker, the kabadiwala and the recycling factory.
I can mend something, and make something new and useful from waste.
I can compare results in a table and a bar chart, and use them to decide which bag or material is best.
I can say what scientists agree about waste and plastic, and what they still argue about, such as plastic-eating microbes and whether recycling is enough.

terms.meaning: Anything we have stopped using and throw out.
terms.example: Peels, wrappers, old newspapers and a broken pen are all waste in most homes.
terms.art: A kitchen dustbin with a peel, a wrapper, a newspaper and a broken pen peeking out.

terms.meaning: To make less waste in the first place. It is the most important of the three Rs.
terms.example: Carrying a cloth bag to the market, so you don't need a plastic one.
terms.art: A child with a cloth bag at a vegetable cart, waving away an offered plastic bag.

terms.meaning: To use a thing again, for the same job or a new one.
terms.example: A glass jam jar becomes a jar for storing rava.
terms.art: An empty jam jar, then the same jar full of pale rava on a kitchen shelf.

terms.meaning: To mend a broken thing so it works again.
terms.example: Sewing a button back on a shirt. Fixing a bicycle puncture.
terms.art: A puncture-repair man by the roadside dipping a cycle tube in a tub of water to find bubbles.

terms.meaning: To break a used thing down into its material, and make something new from that material.
terms.example: Old newspapers are soaked and mashed into pulp, and made into new paper.
terms.art: A pile of old newspapers, an arrow, a tub of grey pulp, an arrow, a fresh roll of paper.

terms.meaning: To say no to something you don't need, so it never becomes waste.
terms.example: Saying 'No straw, please' when you buy a juice.
terms.art: A child's hand pushing away a plastic straw next to a glass of juice.

terms.meaning: When tiny living things feed on a dead plant or animal and break them down. What is left becomes part of the soil. Scientists call it decomposing.
terms.example: A fallen mango left under a tree turns soft, brown and then disappears into the soil.
terms.art: A fallen mango shown four times, each softer and browner, until only a dark patch of soil is left.

terms.meaning: Able to be rotted by tiny living things. Things that were once alive are usually biodegradable.
terms.example: Banana peels, cotton cloth and paper are biodegradable. Most plastic is not.
terms.art: A banana peel, a cotton rag and a paper cup with small green leaf badges, and a plastic bottle without one.

terms.meaning: A living thing far too small to see without a microscope. Bacteria and many fungi are microbes.
terms.example: One pinch of garden soil holds many millions of microbes.
terms.art: A pinch of soil on a fingertip, with a zoomed-in circle full of tiny rod-shaped bacteria and thread-like fungi.

terms.meaning: A living thing that feeds on dead plants and animals and breaks them down. Fungi, bacteria and earthworms are decomposers.
terms.example: The white fluffy mould on an old piece of bread is a fungus decomposing the bread.
terms.art: An earthworm, a mushroom and a cluster of bacteria around a rotting leaf.

terms.meaning: A tiny group of atoms joined together. Everything is made of molecules, far too small to see.
terms.example: Sugar is made of sugar molecules. Each one has 45 atoms joined together.
terms.art: A sugar cube with a zoom into one molecule shown as a cluster of coloured balls.

terms.meaning: A very long molecule made of many small pieces joined in a chain, like beads on a string.
terms.example: Starch in rice, cellulose in paper, and the plastic in a bottle are all polymers.
terms.art: A long necklace of identical beads, labelled with tiny pictures of rice, paper and a bottle.

terms.meaning: A material made in factories, mostly from oil or gas. It is made of polymers, very long chain molecules.
terms.example: Milk packets, bottles, buckets and toothbrushes are made of plastic.
terms.art: A row of plastic things: a milk packet, a bottle, a bucket and a toothbrush.

terms.meaning: A tiny tool inside living things that cuts molecules apart or joins them. Each enzyme fits only certain molecules, like a key fits only certain locks.
terms.example: Your spit has an enzyme that cuts starch into sugar. That is why rice tastes sweet if you chew it for a long time.
terms.art: A key-shaped molecule fitting into a lock-shaped gap in a long chain, snipping it.

terms.meaning: A piece of plastic smaller than a grain of rice, often far too small to see. Big plastic slowly breaks into microplastics, but does not rot away.
terms.example: Scientists have found microplastics in the deep sea, in Himalayan snow and in drinking water.
terms.art: A bottle cracking into smaller and smaller pieces, down to specks like dust.

terms.meaning: A big place where a city piles up waste it does not use. A landfill is a dumping ground built so that its waste is covered and its dirty water is caught.
terms.example: Ghazipur in Delhi is one of India's biggest dumping grounds.
terms.art: A huge grey hill of mixed waste with birds circling and trucks queueing at its foot.

terms.meaning: A gas made when wet waste rots without air, such as deep inside a dump. It can catch fire, and it warms the planet.
terms.example: Fires that smoulder for days in dumping grounds are often fed by methane.
terms.art: A cut-away view of a dump with bubbles of gas rising from rotting food deep inside.

terms.meaning: A person who buys old newspapers, bottles, metal and some plastic from homes, and sells them on to be recycled.
terms.example: The kabadiwala weighs your old newspapers on a scale and pays you for them.
terms.art: A kabadiwala with a hand cart and a hanging scale, weighing a bundle of newspapers at a door.

terms.meaning: A person who collects and sorts things others have thrown out, and sells them for recycling. In Indian cities, many waste pickers are women.
terms.example: In Pune, waste pickers collect sorted waste from lakhs of homes, door to door.
terms.art: A woman in a green apron sorting bottles, paper and cans into big sacks.

terms.meaning: Dark, crumbly soil made when peels, leaves and other once-living things rot. It is food for plants.
terms.example: A pot of peels and dry leaves turns into compost in about two to three months.
terms.art: A hand holding dark crumbly compost with a tiny seedling growing out of the compost.

terms.meaning: To turn waste into something more useful or more beautiful than it was.
terms.example: Old saris stitched together into a warm kantha quilt.
terms.art: A pile of faded saris, then a quilt with rows of running stitches.

terms.meaning: To recycle a thing into something of lower quality, which often cannot be recycled again.
terms.example: A plastic bottle is often recycled into polyester thread for a T-shirt. The T-shirt is hard to recycle again.
terms.art: A clear bottle, an arrow, a fluffy fibre, an arrow, a T-shirt, then a question mark.

explanations.concept: What waste is, and why nature has almost none
explanations.definition: Waste is anything we have stopped using and throw out. In nature, almost nothing is wasted, because one living thing's leftovers are another living thing's food.
explanations.description: In a forest, the leftovers of one living thing are food for another. Earthworms eat fallen leaves. Dung beetles feed their young on dung. Fungi and bacteria break dead things down, and what is left feeds new plants. So the same materials are used again and again. People make waste in two ways a forest does not. We make materials, like plastic, that almost nothing can eat. And we mix things together, so even useful things get spoiled. Because people make this waste, people can also make less of it.
examples: A fallen leaf feeds earthworms, which turn it into soil for the tree.
A banana peel thrown on soil disappears in a few weeks.
A plastic wrapper thrown on the same soil is still there years later.
explanations.art: A forest floor loop: a falling leaf, an earthworm eating the leaf, dark soil, a seedling growing, and to one side a plastic wrapper lying outside the loop.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the unit: what waste is, and why a forest makes almost none.

explanations.concept: Reduce first, then reuse and repair, then recycle
explanations.definition: There are three main ways to make less waste: reduce, reuse and recycle. Reduce comes first, reuse and repair come next, and recycle comes last.
explanations.description: Making anything uses up materials, water and energy. A plastic bag needs oil, a factory and a truck. Reducing means that bag is never made at all. So nothing is used up, and nothing has to be thrown out. Reusing and repairing keep a thing working for longer. Recycling is good too, but it comes last. It needs collecting, sorting, washing, melting and trucks. And a little of the material is lost each time. Some people add more Rs. Refuse means saying no to things you don't need. Repurpose means using a thing for a new job. Together these are often called the 5Rs.
examples: Reduce: carry a steel water bottle instead of buying a plastic one.
Reuse: a glass jar becomes a pencil holder.
Repair: the cobbler stitches a torn chappal strap.
Recycle: the kabadiwala takes old newspapers to be made into new paper.
explanations.art: A staircase of four steps labelled with pictures: a cloth bag at the top, then a glass jar, then a needle and thread, then a recycling factory at the bottom.
explanations.context: People often say reduce, reuse, recycle. This card explains why the order matters.

explanations.concept: Why peels rot: microbes and their enzymes
explanations.definition: A peel rots because microbes, such as bacteria and fungi, feed on the peel. They use enzymes, tiny cutting tools, to cut its long molecules into small pieces they can eat.
explanations.description: A banana peel is made of long chain molecules, such as cellulose and starch. Microbes in the soil feed on them. But a microbe has no mouth, and cannot swallow a whole chain. So they pour out enzymes all around them. Each enzyme is shaped to fit one kind of chain, like a key fits a lock. It snips the chain into small pieces. The microbe soaks the pieces in as food. What is left over becomes part of the soil. Microbes have been feeding on dead plants and animals for hundreds of millions of years. So for almost everything that was once alive, some microbe somewhere has the right enzyme. Warmth, water and air help them work faster. That is why peels rot quickly in a warm, damp pot, and slowly in a dry desert.
examples: Bread left in a damp box grows white and green fluffy mould. That mould is a fungus eating the bread.
Leaves under a tree turn into dark soil in the monsoon.
Chew a mouthful of plain rice for a long time and it starts to taste sweet. An enzyme in your spit is cutting starch into sugar.
explanations.art: A zoom in four steps: a banana peel in soil, threads of fungus on the peel, a single microbe releasing tiny scissor-shaped enzymes, and the enzymes snipping a long chain into small beads.
explanations.context: In the jar test, the peel rots first. This card zooms in to show what is really eating it.

explanations.concept: Why most plastic does not rot
explanations.definition: Most plastics do not rot because microbes have almost no enzymes that fit their molecules. Plastic molecules are a new kind of long chain. Most plastic has been made only in the last 75 years.
explanations.description: A plastic bag is made of very long chain molecules, mostly of carbon and hydrogen atoms. Their atoms hold on to each other very strongly. The chains pack tightly, and water cannot soak in. Microbes have had hundreds of millions of years to evolve enzymes for leaves, wood and bones. Most plastic has existed for less than 75 years. Almost no microbe has an enzyme that fits plastic. So a plastic bag in the soil just sits there. Sunlight and heat slowly crack it into smaller and smaller pieces. But tiny pieces are still plastic. Nobody has watched a bag for hundreds of years. So times on posters, like '450 years for a bottle', are rough guesses from tests.
examples: A milk packet in the jar test looks the same after two weeks.
Old plastic buckets left in the sun go pale and brittle and crack. They do not turn into soil.
Leo Baekeland made Bakelite, one of the first plastics made entirely from chemicals, in 1907. Most of the plastic in the world has been made since 1950.
explanations.art: Two chains side by side under a magnifier: a peel chain with keyhole-shaped gaps that enzyme keys fit into, and a smooth plastic chain with no keyholes and an enzyme key bouncing off.
explanations.context: In the jar test, the plastic does not change at all. This card explains why, by zooming in to its molecules.

explanations.concept: Plastic breaks into microplastics, which travel everywhere
explanations.definition: Microplastics are pieces of plastic smaller than a grain of rice. Big plastic things break into them slowly, in sunlight, heat and rubbing.
explanations.description: In 2004, the British scientist Richard Thompson and his team gave these tiny pieces a name: microplastics. Since then, scientists have looked for them almost everywhere, and found them. They are in the deepest parts of the ocean. In 2019, climbers on Mount Everest collected snow on the way up. The British scientist Imogen Napper and her team tested it. They found microplastics as high as about 8,400 metres, close to the top. Wind, rivers and rain carry them. Fish, birds, turtles and tiny sea animals swallow them by mistake, along with their food. Scientists have also found them inside people. What they do inside bodies is still being studied.
examples: A polyester T-shirt sheds tiny plastic threads every time it is washed.
Car tyres wear away into tiny rubber and plastic bits on the road.
Seabirds have been found with stomachs full of plastic pieces.
explanations.art: A world map with tiny glittering specks along rivers, in the sea, on a snowy Himalayan peak and inside a fish, a seabird and a turtle.
explanations.context: If plastic does not rot, where does it end up? This card follows it into tiny pieces that travel the world.

explanations.concept: Where waste really goes in an Indian city
explanations.definition: City waste goes along two main roads. Mixed waste is taken to a dumping ground. Sorted waste can be composted or sold for recycling, much of it by waste pickers and kabadiwalas.
explanations.description: India's towns and cities throw out more than a lakh tonnes of waste every day. About half of it is wet waste, like peels and leftover food. The rest is dry: paper, plastic, metal, glass and cloth. When it is all mixed in one bag, the wet part soaks and spoils the paper. Then most of it goes to a dumping ground on the edge of the city. Ghazipur in Delhi began in 1984. By 2019 its hill of waste was about 65 metres high, almost as tall as the Qutub Minar. Inside dumps like this, wet waste rots without air and makes methane gas. It catches fire, and the smoke harms the people and animals nearby. When waste is sorted at home, it goes a better way. Wet waste can become compost or cooking gas. Dry waste is picked up by waste pickers and kabadiwalas. They sort it and sell it on to recycling factories. Indore, in Madhya Pradesh, sorts almost all its waste. It has been ranked India's cleanest city again and again since 2017.
examples: A cow on the street eats a plastic bag with food inside. The plastic can block her stomach.
A rinsed, dry milk packet can be sold. A milk packet full of sour milk and peels usually ends up in the dump.
In 2016, India made a rule that every home should sort its waste into wet, dry and hazardous.
explanations.art: A map of a city with two roads leading from a home: one road with a mixed bag going to a smoking grey dump hill beside a tower like the Qutub Minar, and one road with two sorted bins going to a compost yard and a kabadiwala's shop and a factory.
explanations.context: We put waste out, and it disappears from our lane. This card follows it to the real places it goes.

explanations.concept: How recycling works, material by material
explanations.definition: Recycling breaks a used thing down into its material and makes something new from it. Metal and glass can be melted and remade again and again. Paper and most plastics get a little weaker each time.
explanations.description: Metal cans are melted in a furnace and poured into new shapes. Metal atoms do not wear out, so this can happen almost for ever. Making a can from old aluminium cans takes only about a twentieth of the energy of making it from rock. Glass bottles are crushed and melted into new glass. Paper is soaked and mashed into pulp. Its tiny fibres come from wood, and they get shorter each time. After about five to seven times, they are too short to hold together. Plastic is the hardest. There are many kinds, and they cannot be melted together. Thin wrappers and shiny chip packets, made of layers of plastic and metal, are very hard to recycle at all. In India, many old PET bottles are shredded into flakes and spun into polyester fibre. That fibre fills pillows and becomes cloth. This is called downcycling, because the new thing is hard to recycle again.
examples: A steel tiffin can be melted and remade into a new steel spoon.
Old notebooks become egg trays and cardboard.
A PET bottle becomes polyester fibre for a jacket or a pillow.
explanations.art: Four little factory loops: a can circling back into a can, a bottle circling back into a bottle, paper circling a few times and getting thinner, and a plastic bottle going once into a T-shirt and stopping.
explanations.context: What does a factory actually do with old cans, bottles, paper and plastic? This card explains, one material at a time.

explanations.concept: The people who really recycle: waste pickers and kabadiwalas
explanations.definition: In India, most recycling is done by people working outside the city's own system. They are waste pickers, kabadiwalas and small scrap dealers.
explanations.description: Waste pickers walk streets and dumps collecting paper, plastic, glass and metal that others threw out. They sort it by hand and sell it. Many of them are women. Kabadiwalas buy sorted waste from homes and sell it to bigger dealers, who sell it to factories. Together they recover a large share of the things in India that are recycled. For a long time they were chased away and treated as dirty, as if the waste were theirs. In 1993, waste pickers in Pune, most of them women, formed a union, the Kagad Kach Patra Kashtakari Panchayat. Two women, Poornima Chikarmane and Laxmi Narayan, helped them begin it. Later, the waste pickers set up a cooperative called SWaCH. Its members collect sorted waste door to door from many homes in Pune. India's 2016 waste rules say waste pickers should be included in city waste work. Their work is still often unsafe and poorly paid.
examples: The kabadiwala knows by touch which plastic sells and which does not.
A waste picker can sort a sack of mixed waste into more than ten kinds.
Rinsing and drying a milk packet makes it worth something to a waste picker.
explanations.art: A group of women waste pickers in green aprons at a sorting shed, sorting a heap into sacks marked with drawings of a bottle, a can, a newspaper and a glass jar.
explanations.context: When a bottle is recycled in India, who actually does the work? This card is about them.

explanations.concept: India's old ways of reuse and repair
explanations.definition: Reuse and repair are old habits in many Indian homes. People mended, passed on and remade things until they were truly worn out.
explanations.description: In Bengal, old saris were layered and stitched with tiny running stitches into kantha quilts. In Maharashtra, they became godhadi quilts. Torn clothes were darned by a rafoogar, a mender who weaves new thread into a hole so it almost disappears. Steel tiffins and brass pots lasted a lifetime, and were then sold for their metal. Food was served on leaf plates made of sal or banana leaves, and tea in clay kulhads. These go back to the soil. Street-corner repairers still fix cycles, shoes, umbrellas, pressure cookers and phones. In Japan, people mend broken pots with gold lacquer, so the cracks shine. This is called kintsugi. Today, some countries are passing 'right to repair' rules, so that companies must let people fix the things they buy. In 2022, India's government started a right to repair website.
examples: A cobbler stitches a new sole onto an old shoe.
Old cotton dhotis become dusters, then wicks, then compost.
A cracked plate mended with gold lines, in the Japanese way.
explanations.art: A row of repairs: a kantha quilt with running stitches, a rafoogar darning a shawl, a cobbler under an umbrella, and a cup with shining gold cracks.
explanations.context: Long before the word recycling, many Indian homes reused and repaired almost everything. This card looks at how.

explanations.description: In 2016, a team of Japanese scientists led by Shosuke Yoshida and Kohei Oda made a surprise discovery. Near a bottle recycling plant in the city of Sakai, they found a bacterium living on PET plastic, the plastic of drinking bottles. They named this bacterium Ideonella sakaiensis. Ideonella makes two enzymes that cut PET into small pieces, and then eats the pieces. Ideonella is slow, and took about six weeks to eat a thin film of plastic. Scientists have since changed these enzymes to make them faster. And in 2017, Federica Bertocchini, an Italian scientist working in Spain, noticed that wax worms, the young of a moth, chewed holes in a plastic bag. She and her colleagues found that they seem to break down polyethylene, the plastic of most bags. How much they truly digest is still argued about.
examples: A bacterium found near a Japanese recycling plant feeds on bottle plastic.
Wax worms, which normally eat beeswax in beehives, chew through plastic bags.

perspectives.explanation: Life is already finding ways to eat plastic, in less than a hundred years. Improved enzymes can turn old bottles back into the building blocks of new plastic. In France, a company called Carbios has already tested this in a small factory.

These enzymes work mainly on PET, only one of many plastics. They need warmth and clean, shredded plastic in a tank. They cannot clean the sea or a dump. And some tests on worms may have measured the worm's own body, not digested plastic.
Even if microbes help one day, waiting for them is not a plan. Reducing plastic still matters most. These microbes did not evolve to help us. They are simply feeding, as living things do.

explanations.art: A tiny rod-shaped bacterium on a sheet of clear plastic, nibbling a small hole, beside a wax worm poking through a plastic bag.
explanations.context: Can any living thing eat plastic? This card is about a real discovery from 2016, and why scientists still argue about what it means.

explanations.concept: When wood would not rot: an old puzzle
explanations.description: Wood is tough because it holds a very tough molecule called lignin. Only some fungi, called white-rot fungi, have strong enzymes to break it down. About 360 to 300 million years ago, long before dinosaurs, huge swamp forests grew. Many of their fallen trees did not rot. They were buried and squashed, and over millions of years they became coal. So why didn't they rot? Scientists disagree.
examples: A fallen log in a forest takes years to rot, much longer than a leaf.
The coal burned in Indian power stations is made of plants that lived millions of years ago.

perspectives.who: Dimitrios Floudas and his colleagues, in 2012
perspectives.explanation: They studied the genes of many fungi. They suggested that fungi that could rot lignin only evolved near the end of that time. Before that, much wood had no decomposer, a bit like plastic today.

perspectives.who: Matthew Nelsen and his colleagues, in 2016
perspectives.explanation: They argued that lignin-eating life existed earlier. They think the coal formed because of wet swamps and sinking land, where fallen trees were buried quickly in water with little air.
Both parts may matter. Either way, the story shows that new materials can stay around until life finds a way to eat them, or until they are buried.

explanations.art: An ancient swamp forest with giant fern-like trees, fallen trunks lying in dark water, and below them a cut-away of layers turning into black coal.
explanations.context: Plastic is not the first material that life could not eat. This card is about wood, long ago, and an argument about coal.

explanations.concept: Nothing is destroyed: atoms only move
explanations.definition: When things rot, burn or are recycled, their atoms are not destroyed. The atoms are only rearranged and moved somewhere else.
explanations.description: In 1789, the French chemist Antoine Lavoisier published careful tests showing this. He weighed everything before and after burning things in sealed containers. The total weight stayed the same. His wife and fellow scientist, Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier, worked beside him. She kept lab notes, drew the equipment for his book, and translated English science papers for him. So a peel that rots does not vanish. Its atoms become microbes, soil, water and air. A plastic bag that burns does not vanish. It becomes smoke, harmful gases and ash. The carbon in plastic has its own long story. Oil formed from tiny sea plants and animals that lived millions of years ago. So plastic is made of very old life, joined in a new way that today's life can hardly eat.
examples: Weigh a sealed jar of peels and soil today and in two weeks. The weight hardly changes, even though the peel rots.
Burning garbage makes smoke that we breathe, and ash that stays.
explanations.art: A balance scale with a sealed jar of peels on each side, one fresh and one rotted, perfectly level. Beside it, a small portrait-style drawing of Marie-Anne and Antoine Lavoisier at a lab bench.
explanations.context: When we throw something 'away', or burn it, does it really disappear? This card explains what happens to its atoms.

explanations.concept: Is waste a thing, or a label?
explanations.description: A broken bangle is waste to the girl who broke it. It is precious to an artist who makes a mosaic. A peel is waste in the kitchen and food in the compost pot. So some thinkers say waste is not a kind of thing at all. It is a name we give to a thing in the wrong place, or one nobody has found a use for yet. This is an idea, not a science fact. Others disagree.
examples: Nek Chand built a whole garden in Chandigarh from broken tiles, bangles and sinks. It opened to the public in 1976.
Cow dung is waste on a road, but fuel, plaster and fertiliser in many villages.

perspectives.who: Mary Douglas, a British thinker, in her book Purity and Danger, 1966
perspectives.explanation: She wrote that dirt is 'matter out of place'. What counts as dirt depends on the order a group of people have made.

perspectives.who: People who design for a 'circular economy'
perspectives.explanation: Things should be designed from the start so that every part can be reused, repaired, recycled or composted. Then there is no waste at all.
Some waste really is harmful wherever you put it, like old batteries, tube lights with mercury and hospital needles. Calling it a label does not make it safe.

explanations.art: One broken green bangle shown twice: in a dustbin, and set into the skirt of a mosaic dancer sculpture.
explanations.context: This card asks a thinking question: is waste really a kind of thing, or just a word we use?

agreed.text: Things that were once alive, like peels, paper and cotton, are rotted by microbes. Most plastics are not.
agreed.evidence: Bury tests, done by scientists and by children, show peels and paper breaking down while plastic stays the same. Scientists have found and studied the enzymes that microbes use to do the cutting.

agreed.text: Reducing waste is better than recycling it.
agreed.evidence: Studies that add up all the energy, water and materials used show that a thing never made saves the most. Recycling saves a lot too, but collecting, washing and melting need energy, and some material is lost.

agreed.text: Sorting waste at home makes it far easier to compost and recycle.
agreed.evidence: Cities that sort, such as Indore, send far less waste to dumps. Mixed waste spoils paper and hides recyclable things under food.

agreed.text: Burning plastic and garbage harms health.
agreed.evidence: Smoke from burning plastic has tiny soot particles and poisonous gases. Doctors link this kind of smoke to lung and heart illness.

agreed.text: Only a small share of all plastic ever thrown out has been recycled.
agreed.evidence: In 2017, three American scientists added up all the plastic made in the world up to 2015. They were Roland Geyer, Jenna Jambeck and Kara Lavender Law. Of all the plastic that had become waste, about 9 out of every 100 parts had been recycled. About 12 had been burned. About 79 were in dumps, or loose in nature.

challenging.claim: Burning garbage makes it go away.
challenging.who: Many people who burn leaves and garbage on the roadside
challenging.for: After burning, the heap is much smaller. It looks gone.
challenging.against: Atoms are never destroyed. Burning turns waste into smoke, harmful gases and ash. The smoke goes into our lungs and the lungs of birds and animals nearby. Burnt plastic makes some of the most harmful smoke of all.
challenging.context: Sometimes people burn heaps of garbage. This card asks whether burning really gets rid of it.

challenging.who: Labels on some bags sold as biodegradable
challenging.for: Some bags are made to break down. Some do break down in hot industrial compost yards.
challenging.against: In 2019, Imogen Napper and Richard Thompson, two British scientists, left different bags in soil, in the sea and in open air for three years. Some 'biodegradable' bags buried in soil or left in the sea could still carry a full load of shopping after three years. Labels can promise more than a bag can do.
challenging.context: Some plastic bags say 'biodegradable' on them. This card is about a test of whether that is true.

challenging.claim: Recycling will solve the plastic problem.
challenging.who: Many companies that make plastic things and packaging
challenging.for: Recycling keeps material in use. Better sorting machines and new enzyme methods are improving it.
challenging.against: Only about 9 out of every 100 parts of plastic waste ever made have been recycled. Many kinds, like chip packets, are hardly recycled at all. Many scientists and environment groups say we must make and use much less plastic as well.
challenging.context: This card is about a big argument: can recycling deal with all our plastic, or must we use much less?

challenging.claim: A cloth bag is always better for the planet than a plastic bag.
challenging.for: Cloth bags last for years and don't become microplastic litter. Plastic bags harm animals, block drains and last for centuries.
challenging.against: Growing cotton takes lots of water, land and energy. A 2018 study for the Danish government looked at this. A cotton bag must be used many times before it is better for the climate than a thin plastic bag. By one measure, it is more than 50 times. So the best bag is the one you already have, used again and again.
challenging.context: This card compares cloth bags and plastic bags, and asks what 'better' really means.

challenging.claim: Waste pickers are dirty people who make a mess of bins.
challenging.who: An old prejudice in many cities
challenging.for: Waste pickers are seen near dumps and bins, handling dirty things.
challenging.against: Waste pickers clean up what others threw out, and they do much of India's recycling. The dirt comes from the people who mixed and dumped the waste. Pune's waste pickers, most of them women, proved this when they organised and began collecting waste door to door.
challenging.context: This card is about how people who handle waste are often treated, and what the evidence shows.

challenging.claim: Plastic-eating microbes will soon clean up the planet.
challenging.for: Real bacteria, fungi and wax worms have been found that break down some plastics. Scientists keep making their enzymes faster.
challenging.against: The known enzymes work best on one kind of plastic, in warm tanks, on clean shredded pieces. They cannot reach plastic spread through the sea and soil. Most scientists say they may help recycling, but not clean up nature.
challenging.context: Some microbes can eat plastic. This card asks whether that will fix the plastic problem.

challenging.claim: India recycles most of its plastic.
challenging.who: Some reports by government and industry groups
challenging.for: Waste pickers and kabadiwalas collect huge amounts of bottles, buckets and hard plastic, and sell them for recycling.
challenging.against: Nobody counts the work of waste pickers carefully, so the numbers are guesses. Thin wrappers and multi-layer packets are rarely recycled. Much of what is recycled is downcycled once and then thrown out.
challenging.context: This card is about how much of India's plastic really gets recycled, and how hard it is to count.

big_questions.q: When we throw something away, where is 'away'?
big_questions.hint: Follow one wrapper in your mind. Where is it tomorrow? In ten years?

big_questions.q: Why can a microbe eat a peel but not a plastic packet?
big_questions.hint: Think of keys and locks. What happens when someone invents a brand-new lock?

big_questions.q: If atoms are never destroyed, can anything really be thrown out?
big_questions.hint: Where do the atoms of a burnt leaf go?

big_questions.q: Long ago, wood may have piled up because few living things could rot it. Will life learn to eat plastic? Should we wait for it?
big_questions.hint: A bacterium that eats bottle plastic was found in 2016. How fast do you think they work?

big_questions.q: Is a broken thing finished? Who decides when a thing becomes waste?
big_questions.hint: Think of a cracked cup, a torn sari and a broken bangle. What could each become?

big_questions.q: The people who clean up after us are often paid the least. Is that fair?
big_questions.hint: Who cleans your lane? Do you know their name?

big_questions.q: A cow eats plastic, a turtle swallows a bag, a bird feeds plastic to their chicks. Do animals have a right to a clean world, even though they cannot make our laws?
big_questions.hint: Animals cannot vote or write rules. Who should think of them when people make rules about waste?

big_questions.q: Your grandparents made less waste than we do. Were they poorer or richer than us, in ways that matter?
big_questions.hint: Ask an older person you know what they owned, what they mended, and what they threw out.

big_questions.q: Is it better to buy something new and recycle the old one, or to keep the old one for longer?
big_questions.hint: What did making the new one use up?

big_questions.q: A peel feeds microbes, then worms, then a plant. What does a plastic packet feed?
big_questions.hint: Think of your rot jars. Did anything grow on the plastic?

big_questions.q: If everyone in the world lived like your family, how much waste would there be?
big_questions.hint: Weigh one day's dustbin. Now imagine 800 crore people doing the same.

story.title: The Garden of Broken Things
story.note: Nek Chand is real. He was a road inspector in Chandigarh who, from the late 1950s, secretly built a garden of sculptures from broken waste in a patch of forest. Government officials found it in 1975. It was on land where building was not allowed, but the city chose to keep it, and it opened to the public in 1976 as the Rock Garden. Kamla, her mother Bimla, the officer and what they say are made up.
text: In the city of Chandigarh, in the year 1975, there lived a girl called Kamla. She could tell what a thing was made of just by tapping it.

She had learned it from her mother. Bimla collected and sorted the city's waste for a living. Every evening she tipped her sack onto the floor of their one-room house and sorted it in the lamplight. She tapped a bottle with her fingernail. Glass went tink. Plastic went tuk. She dropped a lid on the floor. Tin rang. Steel rang longer. She rubbed a scrap of cloth between her fingers. 'Cotton,' she said. 'This one will go back to the earth. This shiny one never will.'
At school, a boy called Kamla 'kooda-wali', garbage girl, and the others laughed. That evening Kamla asked her mother why she didn't do clean work instead.

Bimla stopped sorting. 'Nothing in this sack is dirty,' she said. 'It is only mixed up. A peel next to a newspaper spoils the newspaper. Put the peel in the earth and the paper in a bundle, and both are useful again.' She held up a cracked cup. 'People say they throw things away. Show me where away is, Kamla, and I will stop working.'
Kamla had no answer.

A few weeks later, at Diwali, Kamla broke her favourite bangles. They were thin green glass, and she had saved for them for months. She slipped on the step, and they snapped into a little heap of curved green pieces. She cried and swept them into her hand to throw out.
'Wait,' said her mother. 'Take them to the thin man with the bicycle.'

Everyone in their part of the city had seen the thin man. He rode a bicycle with sacks tied to the back, and he picked broken things off rubbish heaps. Tiles, bits of sinks, bottle bottoms, smashed cups, broken bangles. Bimla often saved her broken glass for him. People said he was mad. His name was Nek Chand.
Kamla found him at the edge of the forest near the lake, and held out her hand. He looked at the green pieces for a long time. Then he said, 'Can you keep a secret?'
He led her down a narrow path between the trees. Kamla stood still and stared.

Among the trees stood hundreds of statues of people, in rows. There were dancers with skirts made of broken bangles. There were soldiers with faces of broken cups. There were monkeys made of pieces of pipe, and a whole crowd of women carrying pots on their heads, their bodies shining with chips of tile. A grey langur sat on a statue's head and had a good scratch. Lizards ran over the mosaic walls. Birds had nested in a doorway made of an old sink.
'All of this was thrown away,' said Nek Chand. 'When they built this new city, they knocked down the villages that were here before. I brought the villages here.'

Kamla came back every evening after that. She sorted the pieces the way her mother had taught her. She noticed that Nek Chand never used peels or leaves or paper. 'Those rot in the rain,' he said. 'I only use things that do not rot. That is why the garden will last.' Kamla pressed her green bangle pieces into the skirt of a dancer, one by one.
Then one morning, men in uniforms came through the trees with notebooks and long measuring tapes. They looked at the statues the way people look at a pile of rubbish.
'This is government land,' said the officer in charge. 'Nobody is allowed to build here. This is all waste. It must be cleared away.'
Nek Chand said nothing. His face had gone grey. Kamla felt her own face grow hot. She was only ten, and nobody had asked her anything. But she heard her mother's voice in her head.
'Cleared away where?' she said.
The officer looked down at her, surprised.

'Where will you take it?' Kamla said. Her voice shook, but she kept going. 'It doesn't rot. Not one piece of it. Glass doesn't rot, and tile doesn't rot. If you take it away, it will just go to the big dump outside the city. It will sit there for hundreds of years, and be rubbish for all of them.' She pointed at her dancer. 'Here, it is a garden.'
Nobody spoke. A bird called from the sink doorway.

The officer walked slowly along the rows of statues. He stopped in front of the women carrying pots. He bent down and touched a broken tile with a blue pattern. 'My mother had a floor like this,' he said quietly, 'in our village. Before the city came.'

Word spread. People came from all over Chandigarh to see the secret garden in the forest. They found their old villages in it, and their broken cups, and their children's bangles. Some argued that rules were rules. Many more said the garden must stay. In the end, the city decided to keep it. In 1976, it opened to everyone.

Nek Chand kept building for the rest of his long life. Today millions of people have walked through his garden. Most of them never notice one dancer in a far corner, whose skirt is made of pieces of green bangles.
Kamla noticed. And every evening she helped her mother sort the city's sacks, tink and tuk, cotton and shiny, so that less of it went to the dump.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the turn comes when Kamla asks 'cleared away where?'. Glass, tile and ceramic do not rot, so there is no away for them. They can only become a dump or become something else. The same property that makes some waste a problem, that it lasts, is what makes it perfect for a garden that lasts. Bimla's lesson is the other half: waste is mostly things mixed up and in the wrong place. Sorted, they are useful again.
ask: Kamla asked the officer, 'Cleared away where?' Why was that such a good question?
Why did Nek Chand use only glass, tile and broken cups, and never peels or paper?
Bimla said that nothing in her sack was dirty, only mixed up. What did she mean?
The boy at school called Kamla 'garbage girl'. Who do you think was really the expert on waste in this story?
Langurs, lizards and birds lived in the garden too. Who else might a garden made of waste be for?

games.title: Where Does It Go?
games.context: This is a card game about waste. Each card shows a thing people throw out. Players choose the best place for it: reduce, reuse, repair, compost, the kabadiwala, a special collection point for hazards, or, only if nothing else works, the dump. The best place is written on the back of each card.

printables.title: 30 waste cards to cut out (the best place is on the back)

items.b: COMPOST. Microbes in the soil turn it into soil.
REUSE. It can store rava, dal or pencils.
KABADIWALA. It is sold and made into new paper.
REDUCE. Say 'No straw, please', so it is never used.

items.f: A shirt with a missing button
items.b: REPAIR. Five minutes with a needle and thread, and the shirt works again.
KABADIWALA. Clean, dry plastic can be sold and recycled.
DUMP. Its layers of plastic and metal are stuck together, so almost nobody recycles it. The real answer comes earlier: REDUCE, by not buying it.

items.f: A steel tumbler with a dent
items.b: REPAIR. A dent can be hammered out. Steel lasts a lifetime.
REUSE. It can keep toys or school things.

items.f: Coffee grounds after making filter coffee
items.b: COMPOST. Microbes feed on them and make soil.
HAZARD. It holds harmful chemicals. It must go to a special collection point, never in the dustbin.
REUSE. Press the pieces into a mosaic, as Nek Chand did. If you cannot, wrap them in paper so nobody is cut.

items.f: A cotton T-shirt that is too small
items.b: REUSE. Give it to a younger child, or use it as a duster.
KABADIWALA. Hard plastic is sold on to be recycled.
KABADIWALA. Metal can be melted and made into new cans again and again.

items.f: A cycle tube with a puncture
items.b: REPAIR. A puncture shop finds the hole with bubbles in water and patches it.

items.f: A school notebook with empty pages at the back
items.b: REUSE. Use the empty pages for rough work.
COMPOST. They rot into soil.
REPAIR. A cobbler can stitch it.
COMPOST. Flowers rot into soil.
HAZARD. An old tube light holds a little mercury, a harmful metal. It needs a special collection point.

items.f: A pizza box with cheese stuck on it
items.b: KABADIWALA for the clean lid, COMPOST for the cheesy part. Either answer scores 2.

items.f: A toy car with one wheel missing
items.b: REPAIR. Make or glue on a new wheel, for example from a bottle cap.
REDUCE. Shiny paper cannot be recycled. Wrap gifts in cloth or newspaper instead.
REDUCE. Carry a cloth bag, so you never need it.
COMPOST. They rot into soil.

items.f: TEST IT: knock a glass bottle and a plastic bottle with your fingernail. Can you hear which is which?
items.b: Glass goes tink, a clear ring. Plastic goes tuk, a dull sound. Glass is made from sand, and most plastic from oil.

items.f: TEST IT: hold a cotton rag and a plastic bag. Which one was once a living plant?
items.b: The cotton rag. Cotton grows on a plant, so cotton rots in soil. Most plastic is made from oil, and does not rot.

items.f: TEST IT: look at the bottom of a plastic bottle. Can you find a number inside a triangle of arrows?
items.b: The number tells sorters which kind of plastic it is. A 1 means PET, the plastic of most drinking bottles. It does not promise that the bottle will be recycled.

items.f: TEST IT: name one thing in this room that has been repaired.
items.b: Any real answer scores: stitched cloth, a glued toy, a mended chair. Say how it was mended.

printables.title: Seven place mats
items: REDUCE: we should not have made or bought it
COMPOST: let it rot into soil
KABADIWALA: sell it to be recycled
HAZARD: needs a special collection point

printables.title: Score sheet: best place 2 points, another good place 1 point, TEST IT winner 2 points

rules: Lay the seven mats in a row. Shuffle the cards and put them face down.
On your turn, take the top card and read the front out loud. Do not turn it over yet.
Put it on the mat you think is best, and say why in one sentence.
Now turn the card over. If the back names your mat, you score 2 points. If you chose a different mat, but your reason is good and the other players agree, you score 1 point. Otherwise you score 0.
A TEST IT card is not placed on a mat. Everyone does the test. The first to explain the result scores 2 points. Then read the back.
When the cards run out, the player with the most points wins. If points are equal, you share the win.
Playing alone: set a timer for 8 minutes and place every card. Then check each one on its back and count your points. Try to beat your score next time.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the seven mats in a row: REDUCE, REUSE, REPAIR, COMPOST, KABADIWALA, HAZARD, DUMP. 2. Shuffle the 30 cards and put them face down. 3. Put the score sheet and a pencil nearby.
flow.say: Every card is something people throw out. For each one, we choose the best place. Then we turn the card over to see what the back says.
flow.kid: Lay out the seven mats in a row. Mix up the cards. Put them face down. For each card, find its best place.
flow.context: This is the first step of Where Does It Go?, a card game about waste. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Find the card 'A shirt with a missing button' in the pile. Play it together first as a practice round, and score it as normal.
flow.say: Let's practise. A shirt with a missing button. Where is the best place for it?
flow.kid: Practice card: a shirt with a missing button. Where should it go? Choose your answer.

ask.q: Why is repair better than the kabadiwala here?
good: Sewing on a button is quick, and the shirt works again.
No new shirt has to be made.

check.q: A shirt with a missing button. What is the best place for it?
check.why: Sewing on one button takes five minutes, and the shirt is as good as new. Picking KABADIWALA often means thinking 'old cloth is for recycling'. But recycling should come only after mending fails. Picking COMPOST means remembering cotton rots, which is true, but the shirt still has years of life in it.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. Each player draws a card, reads it out and places it. 2. They say why. 3. Turn the card over and give the points.
flow.say: Say why before you turn the card over. A good reason can score even when the back names a different place.
flow.kid: Take turns. Read your card. Put it on a mat and say why. Then turn the card over.
flow.parent: Many things have more than one good answer, so give 1 point for a different place with a good reason, and talk about it. Reuse and repair come before the kabadiwala, because then nothing has to be broken down and made again. Hazards such as the battery and the tube light hold harmful chemicals, so they never go in the ordinary dustbin.

flow.do: When a TEST IT card comes up, stop and do the test together. Everyone guesses first. The first to explain the result scores 2 points.
flow.say: Before we test it, everyone guess. Then let's try it.
flow.kid: A TEST IT card! First, guess what will happen. Then try it.

ask.q: The bottle has a number inside a triangle of arrows. What do you think it tells us?
good: Which kind of plastic it is.
It helps people sort plastics for recycling.

flow.parent: The number tells sorters which kind of plastic it is. A 1 means PET, the plastic of most drinking bottles. It does not promise that the bottle will be recycled.
flow.think: Why do you think there are so many kinds of plastic, when there is only one kind of banana peel?

flow.do: 1. Count the points and find the winner. 2. Look at the seven mats together.
flow.say: Look at the mats. Which mat has the most cards? Which cards were the hardest to place?
flow.kid: Add up your points. Who won? Look at the DUMP mat. Could that card have been stopped at the start?
flow.think: Which cards would not exist at all if we reduced first?

games.title: Loops and Ladders
games.context: This is a board game like snakes and ladders, which began in India as Gyan Chaupar, a game about good and bad deeds. In this version, ladders are good ways to deal with waste, and snakes are harmful ones.

printables.title: A 30-square board (5 rows of 6), to draw or print
items: Square 3: LADDER up to 11. You carried a cloth bag to the market. Reduce! Question: Why is a cloth bag better than a new plastic bag each time?
Square 6: LADDER up to 14. You sewed a button back on. Repair! Question: Why is repairing better than buying new?
Square 9: LADDER up to 19. You rinsed the milk packets and sold them to the kabadiwala. Recycle! Question: Why must milk packets be rinsed before selling?
Square 13: SNAKE down to 4. You threw a chips packet out of the bus window. Question: Where does the packet end up, and who has to deal with it?
Square 15: LADDER up to 23. You started a compost pot with peels and dry leaves. Question: What do microbes need to turn peels into compost?
Square 17: SNAKE down to 7. You burned a pile of plastic. The smoke hurt everyone's lungs. Question: What could your family have done with the plastic instead?
Square 20: LADDER up to 28. You gave your old books to a younger child. Reuse! Question: Why does reusing a book save trees?
Square 22: SNAKE down to 12. You mixed peels with newspaper, and the newspaper was spoiled. Question: Why does a wet peel spoil paper?
Square 26: SNAKE down to 16. You threw a plastic bag with food in it on the road. A cow ate the bag. Question: Why can't a cow digest a plastic bag?
Square 29: SNAKE down to 18. You bought a new toy and threw out one that just needed a wheel fixed. Question: What did making the new toy use up?
Square 30: HOME: a clean, green lane

printables.title: One counter for each player, and one dice
items: a bottle cap for each player

rules: Everyone puts a bottle-cap counter on square 1.
On your turn, roll the dice and move that many squares.
If you land at the foot of a ladder, read the sentence and the question on that square out loud. Answer the question, then climb up.
If you land on a snake's head, read the sentence and the question on that square out loud. Answer the question, then slide down.
If you cannot answer, another player or the parent reads the answer from the list. You still climb or slide.
The first player to reach or pass square 30 wins.
Playing alone: play with two counters, a red one for yourself and a blue one for 'the city'. Roll for each in turn. Try to get yours home first, and answer every question.

flow.do: 1. Draw a 5 by 6 grid on a big sheet, numbered 1 to 30 from the bottom. 2. Draw the five ladders and five snakes from the board list. 3. Write each sentence beside its ladder or snake.
flow.say: Snakes and ladders was first played in India, long ago. Ladders were good deeds and snakes were harmful ones. Let's make a waste version.
flow.kid: Draw a grid of 30 squares. Add the ladders and snakes from the list. Write a few words beside each one.
flow.parent: If drawing takes too long, draw only the numbers and arrows, and keep the board list beside you to read from.
flow.context: This is the first step of Loops and Ladders, a waste version of snakes and ladders. Here you make the board.

flow.do: Play in turns. At each ladder or snake, read the sentence and answer the question before moving.
flow.say: Remember, at every ladder and snake you read the sentence and answer the question on that square.
flow.kid: Roll and move. On a ladder or a snake, answer the question first. Then climb or slide.

check.q: You land on the snake: 'You burned a pile of plastic.' What happens to the plastic when it burns?
options: It turns into smoke, harmful gases and ash
check.why: Atoms are never destroyed. Burning turns plastic into smoke, gases and ash, and the smoke harms lungs. Picking 'disappears' means thinking a smaller heap means less stuff. The stuff has just gone into the air. Picking 'compost' mixes up burning with rotting, which only works for things that were once alive.

flow.parent: Answers. Cloth bag: it is used hundreds of times, so no new bag is made for each trip. Repair: it needs only a little thread and skill, while a new thing needs materials, energy and transport. Rinse: sour milk smells, brings flies and spoils the other dry waste. Compost: microbes need water, air, warmth and peels or leaves to feed on. Book: a book used again means no new paper is made. Chips packet: it lies on the road or washes into a drain, and does not rot. Plastic: keep it clean and dry for the kabadiwala, and buy less of it. Wet peel: paper goes soggy and dirty, and cannot be recycled. Cow: gut microbes have enzymes for plants, none for plastic, so the bag stays in her stomach. New toy: materials, energy, a factory, a truck and packaging.

flow.do: When someone reaches square 30, stop and talk.
flow.say: Which snake did you hit most? Which ladder would be easiest to climb in our real home this week?
flow.kid: Who won? Which ladder can your family really climb this week? Choose one.
flow.think: In the real world, who slides down the snake when someone throws plastic on the road? Only the thrower, or others too?
