items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 4, and her family buy a new plastic bottle of water every day. Her mother says, "That is fine, because we give the bottles for recycling." Kavya thinks they should fill a steel bottle at home instead. Explain why Kavya's plan is better. Use the word energy or materials.
items.a: Kavya's plan means no new bottle is made at all, so no plastic, oil or energy is used to make one. Recycling still needs trucks, washing, shredding and melting, which all use energy. And many bottles never reach a factory. A steel bottle can be used for years.
items.why: A strong answer says that reducing stops the waste being made, while recycling still uses energy and materials. That is why reduce comes first.

items.p: Match each action to its R.
pairs: Take a steel dabba to the shop for loose dal
Use an old sari as a curtain
Get the mixie's broken blade fixed
Sell old newspapers to the kabadiwala
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Reduce stops the waste being made. Reuse uses a thing again. Repair mends it so it works again. Recycle breaks it down into material for something new.

items.p: Sort these things. Will each one rot in damp soil within a few months, or not?
items.a: see items
items.why: Things that were once part of a living plant, like peels, leaves and paper, are food for soil microbes, so they rot. Steel, glass and plastic are not food for them. Steel may slowly rust, but it does not rot.

items.p: Before the rot jar test, a girl makes a prediction. Which thing should she expect to look most changed after two weeks?
items.why: A banana peel is soft, wet and was alive only days ago, so microbes start on it quickly. Paper and cotton rot too, but more slowly, because their fibres are tough. The milk packet is plastic, and microbes have almost no enzymes for it.
items.context: In the rot jar test, you bury a banana peel, newspaper, cotton cloth and a strip of milk packet in damp soil in clear jars, and watch for two weeks.

items.p: When plastic breaks into tiny pieces, it has rotted away.
items.why: False. Tiny pieces of plastic are still plastic. They are called microplastics, and they spread into soil, water and animals.

items.p: Pooja, a girl in Class 4, says, "Plastic does not rot because it is buried too deep for the microbes to reach." What is wrong with her idea?
opts: Plastic lying on top of the soil does not rot either. The real reason is that almost no microbe has an enzyme that fits plastic
Plastic rots quickly if it is buried deep enough
items.why: A peel buried at the same depth does rot, so depth is not the reason. Microbes can only eat what their enzymes fit, and their enzymes fit peels, not plastic. Plastic left in the sun cracks into pieces, but it still does not rot.

items.p: Dark, crumbly soil made from rotted peels and leaves is called ____.
items.why: Compost is made by microbes and worms, and it feeds plants.

items.p: Why should we rinse a milk packet before giving it to the kabadiwala?
opts: So old milk doesn't go sour and spoil it and the things beside it
items.why: Sour milk smells, attracts flies and spoils paper and other dry waste. A clean, dry packet can be sold and recycled. Picking 'rots faster' mixes up plastic with peels.

items.p: In many Indian streets, cows eat from rubbish heaps. A cow swallows a plastic bag with vegetable peels inside. Explain what can happen to her, and why her stomach cannot deal with the bag.
items.a: Her gut is full of microbes with enzymes that break down grass and peels. None of them has an enzyme that fits plastic. So the peels are digested, but the bag stays in her stomach. Bags can pile up there until she cannot eat properly, and she can become very ill.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea of enzymes: the cow's gut microbes can digest plants but not plastic.

items.p: Which of these is reuse, and not recycling?
opts: Using an empty glass jam jar to store rava
Melting old jars to make new glass
Pulping newspapers to make new paper
items.why: Reuse means using the thing again as it is. The jar is still a jar. Melting, shredding and pulping break a thing down into material, which is recycling. Reuse saves more energy, because nothing has to be broken down and made again.

items.p: Find two things in your home that are being reused. Say what each one was before. Then say what new thing your family did not have to buy because of it.
items.a: An old cotton T-shirt is now a duster. Before, it was a shirt. So we did not have to buy a new duster. A biscuit tin now holds buttons. Before, it held biscuits. So we did not need a new box.
items.why: A strong answer gives two real examples and sees that each reuse means one new thing does not have to be made.

items.p: Draw what you saw in your jars after two weeks: the peel, the paper, the cloth and the milk packet.
items.a: A drawing showing the peel dark and soft or partly gone, the paper soft or torn, the cloth stained, and the milk packet unchanged.
items.why: Drawing what you really saw is how scientists record. Yours may look different, and that is fine.
items.context: In the rot jar test, you buried a peel, paper, cloth and a strip of milk packet in damp soil in clear jars, against the glass.

items.p: Lakshmi, a girl aged 9, and her family are deciding what to do with their old newspapers.

views.says: Sell them to the kabadiwala. They go to a paper mill and become new paper, so fewer trees are cut.
Keep them. We can wrap things in them, line shelves with them and fold them into bags.
Stop buying the paper and read the news on the phone. Then there is no newspaper waste at all.

items.ask: Which plan do you think is best? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one fair point from another plan.
items.a: A strong answer weighs real trade-offs. Recycling saves trees but still uses trucks, water and energy at the mill. Reusing keeps the paper useful for longer, and it can still be recycled later. Reducing comes first in the order of the Rs, but a phone also uses electricity and is hard to recycle. A strong answer picks one plan, gives a reason, and is fair to another.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Each plan avoids some waste, and each has a cost.

items.p: A woman has a bundle of old newspapers, an empty oil tin, a broken plastic bucket and a bag of vegetable peels. Which ONE will the kabadiwala not buy?
items.why: A kabadiwala buys things that factories can remake: paper, metal and hard plastic. They sell them on to dealers. Peels cannot be remade in a factory. They belong in a compost pot, where microbes turn them into soil.

items.p: Paper rots in soil because it is made from wood, which was once part of a living tree.
items.why: True. Paper is made of fibres from wood. Soil microbes have been feeding on wood for millions of years, so they have enzymes that fit it. That is why paper rots, though more slowly than a peel.

items.p: In the rot jar test, a girl puts the peel jar on a sunny windowsill and the milk-packet jar in a cool cupboard. Why is this not a fair test?
opts: She changed two things at once, the material and the place, so she cannot tell which one made the difference
The jars are not the same colour
The milk packet should be in the sun too, so that it rots
items.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. Here the material and the warmth are both different. If the peel rots faster, nobody can tell whether the material or the warm sun caused it.
items.context: In the rot jar test, you bury a banana peel, newspaper, cotton cloth and a strip of milk packet in damp soil in clear jars, and watch for two weeks.

items.p: Look at the made-up results. The newspaper and the cotton cloth both scored 4 on day 14. What does this tell you?
opts: Both rot, but slowly, so two weeks is too short to see much change
They rotted as fast as the banana peel
items.why: A score of 4 means a little of each had gone, so they are rotting. They are made of tough plant fibres, which take microbes longer to cut. Over a few months, both would rot away, but the milk packet would not.
items.context: In the rot jar test, you bury things in damp soil in a clear jar and score how much is left, from 5 (all there) to 0 (gone).

chart.title: Made-up results: how much was left on day 14 (5 means all of it, 0 means none)

items.p: Write a claim, the evidence and your reasoning about plastic and soil, from the rot jar test.
items.a: Claim: plastic does not rot in soil. Evidence: after 14 days, the milk packet strip looked exactly the same, but the peel was dark, soft and half gone. Reasoning: soil microbes have enzymes for peels but not for plastic.
items.why: A good scientific answer has all three parts: what I think, what I saw, and why.
items.context: In the rot jar test, you buried a peel, paper, cloth and a strip of milk packet in damp soil in clear jars and watched for 14 days.

items.p: An enzyme is a tiny tool, made by living things, that fits only certain molecules, like a key fits only one lock. How does this explain why a fungus that rots fallen logs cannot rot a plastic bucket?
opts: The fungus has enzymes that fit wood molecules, but none that fit plastic molecules
The bucket is harder than a log
The bucket is too big for the fungus
items.why: A fungus can only feed on molecules that their enzymes fit. Their enzymes fit wood, so they can rot a log. Plastic molecules are a different shape, so the fungus has no key for that lock.

items.p: A very long molecule made of many small pieces joined in a chain is called a ____.
items.why: Plastic, starch and cellulose are all polymers.

items.p: Why have microbes had trouble learning to eat plastic?
opts: Plastic is poisonous to all life
Most plastic has existed for less than 75 years, too short for most microbes to evolve the right enzymes
Plastic is too hard to see
items.why: Microbes evolved enzymes for leaves, wood and bones over hundreds of millions of years. Plastic is very new. In 2016, scientists found one bacterium that eats bottle plastic, so life is starting to find ways. Picking 'poisonous' is a common belief, but microbes can live on plastic surfaces without eating them.

items.p: One building puts peels, paper and plastic all together in one bag. Why does most of it end up in the dump, even the paper that could have been recycled?
items.a: Once wet peels are mixed in, the paper gets soggy and dirty, and a paper mill cannot use it. Sorting a smelly mixed bag by hand is slow and unpleasant, so most mixed waste is simply dumped. If the building kept wet and dry waste apart, the paper would stay clean and could be sold.
items.why: A strong answer explains that mixing spoils the dry waste and makes sorting hard, so sorting at home is what makes recycling possible.

items.p: Deep inside a big dump, wet waste rots with no air. This makes a gas that can catch fire and warms the planet. The gas is called ____.
items.why: Methane is made when wet waste rots without air. It causes dump fires and warms the planet. When peels are composted with air, the microbes make far less methane.

items.p: Put a plastic bottle's journey in order, as it happens in many Indian cities.
items: You drink from it and put it in the dry waste bag
A waste picker or kabadiwala collects it
A scrap dealer sorts it with thousands of others
A factory shreds it into flakes
The flakes are melted and spun into polyester fibre
a: You drink from it and put it in the dry waste bag
A waste picker or kabadiwala collects it
A scrap dealer sorts it with thousands of others
A factory shreds it into flakes
The flakes are melted and spun into polyester fibre
items.why: Most PET bottles recycled in India become polyester fibre for pillows, cloth and carpets. This is downcycling, because the fibre is hard to recycle again.

items.p: Sort these by how many times they can be recycled.
cats: Again and again, without getting weaker
items: Again and again, without getting weaker
Again and again, without getting weaker
Again and again, without getting weaker
a chips packet made of plastic and foil layers stuck together
items.a: see items
items.why: Metal and glass can be melted and remade almost for ever. Paper fibres get shorter each time, and recycled PET usually becomes fibre that is hard to recycle again. A chips packet has layers of plastic and metal that cannot easily be pulled apart.

items.p: Waste pickers do a large part of India's recycling.
items.why: True. Waste pickers, many of them women, collect and sort huge amounts of paper, plastic, glass and metal that others threw out.

items.p: Melting down a glass bottle and making a new one uses less energy than washing the old bottle and filling it again.
items.why: False. Melting glass needs a furnace hotter than 1,000 degrees. Washing a bottle needs only water and a little heat. That is why reusing comes before recycling: the thing is used again as it is, and nothing has to be made again.

items.p: Match each old way of reuse or repair to what it is.
pairs: a quilt made from old saris
a mender who weaves thread into holes
a clay cup that goes back to the earth
mending pots with gold in Japan
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These are old ways of making things last, or making things that return to the soil.

items.p: Your family's dry waste bag is full of chips packets and thin wrappers. The kabadiwala won't buy them. What could your family do?
items.a: Buy fewer packaged snacks, and eat fruit, roasted chana or home-made snacks instead. Buy loose things in our own containers. That reduces the packets in the first place.
items.why: When something can't be recycled, the answer is to reduce it.

items.p: Atoms are never destroyed. So when a banana peel rots, where do its atoms go?
opts: Into the microbes, the soil, water and air
items.why: The peel's atoms become part of microbes, soil, water and the air. Nothing vanishes. Picking 'vanish' is natural, because we can't see where they go. But careful weighing, since Antoine and Marie-Anne Lavoisier's time, shows matter is never lost.

items.p: A city is arguing about who should sort its waste into wet and dry.

views.says: Every home must sort its own waste into wet and dry. Once it is mixed, the city cannot compost it or recycle it.

views.who: Mangal, a waste picker in Pune's SWaCH cooperative
views.says: We already sort waste by hand, every day. Pay us fairly and let us collect door to door, and we will do it well.
Give us one bin. A big machine at a factory should do the sorting, so that families do not have to.

items.ask: Whose plan do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one fair point from another person.
items.a: A strong answer uses what the unit shows: mixed waste gets wet and dirty, so sorting at home keeps dry waste clean enough to recycle. It is fair to the waste picker, whose skill does much of India's recycling, and to the mother, who is short of time, even though sorting machines are costly and struggle with wet, mixed waste. A strong answer picks a side, gives a reason, and gives another side its due.
items.why: Pune's waste pickers really did organise and win door-to-door collection work. Many Indian cities now ask homes to sort wet and dry waste. The best answer may combine the plans.

items.p: Long ago, many fallen trees didn't rot and became coal. One idea is that wood-rotting fungi had not evolved yet. What does that idea have in common with plastic today?
opts: Both are new materials that few living things could yet break down
Both are found only in India
items.why: In both cases, a tough material piled up because few decomposers could eat it. This is one idea, and other scientists think swamps burying wood quickly mattered more. Picking 'made by people' is true for plastic, but wood is made by trees.

items.p: A shop says its plastic bag is 'biodegradable'. What is the best scientific thing to do?
opts: Test it: bury it in a jar of damp soil with an ordinary bag and compare after weeks
items.why: A fair test gives evidence. The 2019 study by Imogen Napper and Richard Thompson found that some bags did not rot as promised. Burning only makes harmful smoke.

items.p: Three people are arguing about which shopping bag is best for the planet.

views.says: A thin plastic bag takes very little water and energy to make. It is the lightest choice.
A cotton bag takes a lot of water and energy to make. It is only better if it is used many, many times. But a plastic bag can last for centuries as litter.
The best bag is the one I already have at home, used again and again until it falls apart.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? Use what you found in the bag test or in this unit. Then answer back from one of the other views.
items.a: A strong answer weighs the real costs. Making a cotton bag uses far more water and energy than making a plastic one, so Revathi has a point. But the bag test shows a cloth bag carries much more and lasts for years, and a plastic bag that escapes does not rot. Anjali's view follows the order of the Rs: reusing what you already have avoids making anything new. A strong answer picks a side, backs it with a fact, and is fair to another view.
items.why: Scientists who compare bags find that the answer depends on how many times each bag is used, and on what happens to it at the end. There is no bag that is best in every way.

items.p: Making an aluminium can from old cans takes only about a twentieth of the energy of making one from rock. Explain why recycling saves so much energy here.
items.a: To make a new can from rock, people must dig up the rock, carry it, purify it and use huge amounts of electricity to get the aluminium out. With old cans, the aluminium is already there. It only has to be cleaned and melted. So most of the hard work is skipped.
items.why: A strong answer says which steps recycling skips: digging, purifying and getting the metal out of the rock.

items.p: Recycling a thing into something of lower quality, which often can't be recycled again, is called ____.
items.why: A PET bottle that becomes polyester fibre has been downcycled.

items.p: Ideonella sakaiensis, a bacterium that eats PET bottle plastic, was found near a bottle recycling plant in Japan, where there was plenty of PET to feed on.
items.why: True. Scientists found these bacteria in 2016 near a recycling plant in Sakai, Japan. Living beings often turn up where their food is. Over the years, some microbes there had found a way to feed on PET.

items.p: Glass is made from sand, so a glass bottle thrown in the dump soon turns back into sand.
items.why: False. No microbe can feed on glass, so glass does not rot. It can break into sharp pieces, but each piece is still glass. Only waves rolling it on a beach for many years slowly wear it smooth. Being made from something natural does not mean a thing goes back to nature quickly.

items.p: In the story, Kamla asked the officer, 'Cleared away where?' Explain the science behind her question.
items.a: Glass and tile don't rot, because no microbes can eat them, and their atoms are never destroyed. So taking them away would only move them to the dump, where they would stay for hundreds of years. In the garden, the same pieces were useful and beautiful.
items.why: Her question works because there is no away. Things only move or change form.
items.context: In the story The Garden of Broken Things, officials want to clear away a secret garden of statues made from broken glass and tiles.

items.p: Half of a city's waste is wet waste. If every home composted its wet waste, about how much less would go to the dump?
items.why: If wet waste is about half the total, composting it all would cut the dump's waste by about half. It would also stop most of the methane, which comes from wet waste rotting without air.

items.p: Should a plastic company pay for collecting and recycling the packets it makes? Give one reason for and one against.
items.a: For: the company made the packet and earns money from it, so it should help clean it up. Against: the price of things might go up for everyone.
items.why: This is a real debate. India's plastic rules from 2016 onwards say companies must help collect their plastic packaging. Any well-reasoned answer is good.

items.p: Most waste pickers in Pune's union are women. What did they win by organising together?
opts: Recognition as workers, identity cards, and door-to-door collection work with the city
Their own factory on the Moon
items.why: By organising from 1993, they won identity cards from the city and the right to collect waste door to door through their cooperative, SWaCH. Their work is still hard, and many still fight for fair pay.

items.p: Nobody has watched a plastic bottle for 450 years, so '450 years to break down' is an estimate.
items.why: True. Most plastic has existed for less than 75 years. Times like this are worked out from tests that speed things up, and they are rough guesses.

items.p: Fungi are busy rotting a fallen log. Do they matter for their own sake, or only because they make soil for us? Write what you think and why.
items.a: I think fungi matter for their own sake, because they are alive and feeding, like we are. They also help the forest, and that helps us too.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Every living thing matters for their own sake, not only for what they give us. Some people think a living thing matters mainly for what they do for people.

items.p: Design a better chips packet. It must keep chips crisp, and it must not end up in the dump. Describe or draw it.
items.a: A refillable steel or glass jar that the shop fills from a big tin. Or a paper packet lined with a thin coat that compost microbes can eat.
items.why: Real engineers are working on this problem. Any idea that keeps chips dry and can be reused, recycled or composted is a good answer.

items.p: Waste is sometimes called 'matter out of place'. Give one example of something that is waste in one place and useful in another.
items.a: Cow dung is waste on a road, but fuel and fertiliser in a village. A broken bangle is waste in a dustbin, but art in Nek Chand's garden.
items.why: The saying is old. The thinker Mary Douglas made it famous in 1966. Any real example where place changes usefulness is right.

items.p: A family in Kochi puts all their peels into a compost pot. After three months, the compost weighs much less than all the peels that went in. Atoms are never destroyed, so where did the missing weight go?
opts: Into the air, as carbon dioxide gas and water vapour given off by the microbes as they fed
items.why: As microbes feed on peels, they breathe out carbon dioxide and give off water, just as we do. These float away as gas and vapour. The atoms are not destroyed. They have moved into the air, and plants can take them in again.

experiments.title: The Rot Jar Test: what rots, and what doesn't?
experiments.question: Which of these rots in damp soil: a banana peel, newspaper, cotton cloth or a piece of a milk packet? And why?
experiments.predict: Before you bury anything, put the four things in a line. Put the one you think will rot fastest first, and the one you think will last longest at the end. Then say why you chose that order.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, give each thing its own jar, with the same soil, the same water and the same place. Then only the material is different. Cut each piece about the size of a matchbox, so none has a head start.
results_table: Day 4: how much is left (0 to 5)
Day 8: how much is left (0 to 5)

materials.item: 4 clear glass jars or clear plastic bottles with the top cut off (by a grown-up), all about the same size
soil from a pot where a plant has been growing for some months, or two handfuls from under a tree outside. Not new packaged potting mix or cocopeat.

a piece of banana peel, a strip of newspaper, a scrap of old pure cotton cloth (a handkerchief or an old banian, not polyester) and a strip cut from an empty, rinsed milk packet, each about the size of a matchbox
water in a small cup, a spoon, and a cloth or paper to cover each jar with a rubber band
a marker, 4 labels, gloves (or a spoon for lifting), old newspaper to tip the jars onto, and a magnifying glass if you have one

experiments.safety: Wear gloves or use a spoon when you look closely. Do not sniff the mouldy peel closely, and do not open jars near your face. Wash hands with soap afterwards. A grown-up cuts any plastic bottles.

schedule.what: Make your guesses. Fill four jars with damp soil. Push one thing against the glass in each jar, so you can see it from outside. Cover and label them.
Look through the glass. Score how much of each thing is left, from 5 to 0. Add a spoon of water if the soil looks dry.
Look and score again. Draw what you see.
Score a last time, then tip each jar onto newspaper and look closely. Fill in the table, draw a bar chart and say what you found.

experiments.record: Fill in the table on days 4, 8 and 14. Draw each jar on day 14. Then draw a bar chart with one bar for each thing, as tall as how much was left.

flow.do: 1. Put the peel, newspaper, cloth and milk packet on a plate. 2. Ask your child to line them up, fastest to rot first.
flow.say: We're going to bury these four things and watch them for two weeks. Which do you think will rot first? Put them in a line.
flow.kid: Look at the four things. Which will rot first? Put them in a line, fastest first.

ask.q: Why did you put that one first?
good: The milk packet is plastic, and plastic lasts.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Rot Jar Test. You bury a peel, paper, cloth and a strip of milk packet in clear jars of soil, and watch what tiny living things do to them.

flow.do: 1. Mix the soil with water until it feels like a squeezed sponge: damp, but no water drips out. 2. Fill each jar three-quarters full. 3. Push one thing down against the glass, so you can see it from outside. Keep its top about 3 cm below the soil. 4. Cover it with soil.
flow.say: Soil is full of living things too small to see. They need water and air to work. Damp is good. Soggy is bad, because then they can't breathe.
flow.kid: Make the soil damp like a squeezed sponge. Fill each jar. Push one thing against the glass. Cover it with soil.
flow.parent: Use soil from an old plant pot, or from under a tree. It is full of microbes. New packaged potting mix and cocopeat have far fewer, so things rot much more slowly. If your soil is very dry and dusty, mix in a spoon of old compost.

flow.do: 1. Cover each jar with a cloth or a paper held by a rubber band. 2. Label each jar. 3. Put all four jars together in a warm, shady place, out of direct sun.
flow.say: We keep them all together so they are all just as warm. That keeps the test fair.
flow.kid: Cover each jar. Label it. Put all four jars together in a warm, shady spot.
flow.parent: In a warm month, the peel shows big changes within a week. In a cold north Indian winter, below about 15 degrees, everything is slower. Keep the jars indoors in the warmest room, and leave them for three or four weeks instead of two.

flow.do: On day 4 and day 8, look through the glass with a magnifying glass. Score how much of each thing is left: 5 means all of it, 0 means none. Add a spoon of water to any jar that looks dry.
flow.say: What has changed? Can you see any white threads or fluffy spots? Those are fungi. They are feeding on the peel.
flow.kid: Look through the glass. What has changed? Look for white threads. Score how much is left, from 5 down to 0.
flow.wait: Look again on day 4 and day 8.
flow.parent: Expect the peel to go brown and then black, with white or green mould. The newspaper goes soft and grey. The cloth looks stained. The milk packet looks just the same. If a jar smells bad, it is too wet. Take the cover off for a day to let it dry a little.

flow.do: 1. On day 14, score each jar one last time. 2. Tip each jar onto old newspaper, wearing gloves or using a spoon. 3. Find each thing and look closely. 4. Fill in the table and draw a bar chart.
flow.say: Let's see what's left. Gently, so we don't break anything.
flow.kid: Wear gloves or use a spoon. Tip out each jar. Find your four things. What do they look like now? Draw a bar for each.

check.q: In the rot jar test, the strip of milk packet looked exactly the same after 14 days. Why?
options: Soil microbes have almost no enzymes that can cut plastic molecules
It rotted, but too slowly to see
check.why: Microbes rot things by cutting their molecules with enzymes, and almost none fit plastic. Picking 'buried too deep' means thinking depth was the reason. But the peel was just as deep, and it rotted. Picking 'too slowly to see' is close to the truth for some plastics. But most don't rot at all, they only crack into tiny pieces.

chart.title: Made-up example: how much was left on day 14 (5 means all of it, 0 means none)
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a chart can look like. Yours will be different.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: things that were once alive rot, and plastic doesn't. What I saw: the peel was black and half gone, and the milk packet looked new. Why: tiny living things in the soil feed on peel, but they have no tools for plastic. Put the peel, paper and cloth back into soil or a compost pot for a few months. They will slowly turn into soil. Put the milk packet in the dry waste.
flow.think: If you buried the same plastic and came back when you were grown up, what would you find?

experiments.title: Melt and Remake: new crayons from broken ones
experiments.question: Can broken wax crayons be melted and made into new crayons that still draw? What happens when we mix the colours?
experiments.predict: Before you melt anything, guess. Will the new crayon draw as well as the old one? What colour will you get if you melt red, blue and yellow together? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: To compare fairly, draw ten strokes with an old crayon and ten with your new one, on the same paper, pressing the same way. Keep one mould for a single colour and one for mixed colours, so you can see what mixing does.
results_table: Did it draw well? (yes, a bit, no)

materials.item: a handful of broken wax crayons, with their paper wrappers peeled off
2 small steel bowls and a pan of hot water, for a grown-up to use
a silicone ice tray or chocolate mould, or small cups made by pressing foil around a bottle cap
ice-cream sticks for stirring, and a sheet of paper for testing

experiments.safety: Only a grown-up handles the hot water and the hot bowls. The melted wax is hot enough to burn. Let it cool fully before touching. Never melt crayons directly on a flame, because wax can catch fire.

schedule.what: Peel and sort the crayon pieces. A grown-up melts them in bowls over hot water. Pour into moulds, let them harden, then test them.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Stick a strip of paper with ten strokes from an old crayon and ten from a new one in your notebook.

flow.do: 1. Soak the broken crayons in water for 5 minutes, so the paper peels off easily. 2. Peel off all the paper, and dry the crayons on a cloth. 3. Break the crayons into pieces about the size of a fingernail. 4. Sort them into two piles: one single colour, and one mix of colours (include red, blue and yellow if you have them).
flow.say: These crayons are broken. Most people throw them out. We're going to recycle them, the way a factory recycles metal or plastic.
flow.kid: Peel the paper off the broken crayons. Break them into small bits. Make two piles: one colour, and a mix.
flow.context: This is the first step of Melt and Remake. You melt broken wax crayons and pour them into moulds, to see how recycling by melting works.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up heats a pan of water until it is steaming, not boiling hard. 2. Put each pile of crayon bits in its own steel bowl. 3. Sit the bowls in the hot water. 4. Stir gently with an ice-cream stick until the wax is fully liquid, about 5 to 10 minutes.
flow.say: Wax melts when it's hot, and goes hard again when it cools. Metal, glass and many plastics are recycled the same way, but in furnaces far hotter.
flow.kid: A grown-up melts the wax. Watch it turn from hard bits to a shiny liquid. Don't touch the hot bowls.
flow.parent: This works with ordinary wax crayons. Plastic crayons and oil pastels behave differently: they may not melt, or may stay soft. The water does not need to boil, because crayon wax melts at about 50 to 65 degrees.

flow.do: 1. The grown-up pours the melted wax carefully into the moulds. 2. Leave them to harden for 30 minutes on the table, or 15 minutes in the fridge.
flow.say: Now we wait for the wax to go solid. While we wait, let's guess how the mixed one will look.
flow.kid: A grown-up pours the wax into the moulds. Now wait. What colour will the mix be?
flow.wait: Leave the moulds for about 30 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Pop the new crayons out of the moulds. 2. Draw ten strokes with an old crayon, and ten with a new one, on the same paper. 3. Compare them. 4. Fill in the table.
flow.say: Does the new crayon draw as well as the old one? What happened to the mixed colours?
flow.kid: Pop out your new crayons. Draw ten strokes with an old one. Draw ten with a new one. Which is better?

check.q: Red, blue and yellow crayon bits were melted together. What colour came out?
options: A dull brownish or greyish colour
check.why: Mixed colours blend into a dull brown or grey. This is why recycling factories sort glass by colour and plastics by kind. Mixed materials make a weaker, duller product. Picking 'rainbow' means imagining the colours stay apart. They only stay as stripes if you pour one colour, let it harden, then pour the next.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? And why?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: wax can be recycled by melting, but colours should be sorted first. What I saw: the single-colour crayon drew well, and the mix came out brown. Why: melting lets the wax take a new shape, but it can't un-mix colours. Many plastics are like this too. Each kind melts differently, and mixed kinds make a weak material.

experiments.context: This is the melt and remake test. You melt broken wax crayons in bowls over hot water, pour them into moulds, and test whether the new crayons draw. It shows how recycling by melting works, and why sorting matters.

experiments.title: The Bag Test: which bag carries most?
experiments.question: Which carries the most weight before it tears: a newspaper bag, an old T-shirt bag, a cloth bag or a thin plastic carry bag?
experiments.predict: Before testing, line up the four bags. Put the one you think will carry most first, and the one you think will tear first at the end. Say why you chose that order.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, load every bag the same way: one 1-kilogram weight at a time. Lift each bag by its handles the same height, about a hand's width, and hold it for 10 seconds.
results_table: What broke first: handle, bottom or side?
Could we still use it after the test? (yes or no)

materials.item: a newspaper bag (from activity a5) and a T-shirt bag (from activity a4)
a cloth bag and a thin plastic carry bag that you already have
10 weights of 1 kilogram each: closed 1-litre bottles full of water, or strong sealed 1 kg packets of atta, rice, dal, salt or sugar
a cushion or folded blanket on the floor, and a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Test over a cushion, so falling weights don't crack the floor or hurt toes. Keep feet out from under the bag. A grown-up lifts any bag holding more than 3 kilograms.

schedule.what: Guess. Test each bag by adding one 1-kilogram weight at a time. Write the results. Draw a bar chart and talk about what 'best' means.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each bag, as tall as the kilograms it held.

flow.do: 1. Put the four bags in a row. 2. Ask your child to line them up, strongest first.
flow.say: Which bag do you think will carry the most? Put them in a line, strongest first.
flow.kid: Look at the four bags. Which is strongest? Put them in a line.
flow.context: This is the first step of the bag test. You put 1-kilogram weights into four bags, one at a time, to see which carries most.

flow.do: 1. Put the cushion on the floor. 2. Hold the first bag open over it. 3. Add one 1-kilogram weight. 4. Lift the bag by its handles a hand's width up and hold for 10 seconds. 5. If it holds, add another weight and lift again. 6. When it tears, write down the last number of kilograms it held. 7. Stop at 10 kilograms, and write '10 or more'.
flow.say: One weight at a time. Lift slowly, count to ten, then add another. The number we write is the last one it held safely.
flow.kid: Add one weight. Lift the bag. Count to ten. Did it hold? Add one more. When it tears, write the last number.
flow.parent: A grown-up does the lifting after 3 kilograms. A newspaper bag usually tears first, often at the handles or the pasted bottom. A thin plastic carry bag is often stronger than children expect. That is an honest result, and a good thing to talk about.

flow.do: Draw a bar chart with one bar for each bag.
flow.say: Let's turn the numbers into a picture. A taller bar means the bag carried more.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each bag. Make it as tall as the kilograms it held.

chart.title: Made-up example: how many kilograms each bag held
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your bags will be different.

check.q: In the made-up bag test results, the thin plastic bag held 5 kilograms and the newspaper bag held only 2. Does that mean the plastic bag is the best bag?
options: Not by itself: we must also think how many times it is used, and where it ends up
check.why: Strength is only one thing to think about. A thin plastic bag is often used once, and then lasts for centuries as litter. A newspaper bag is weaker, but it rots. A cloth bag is strong and can be used hundreds of times. Picking 'strongest is always best' means looking at one number only. Picking 'plastic is always weakest' means expecting a result instead of looking at the test.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: What do you think is the best bag now? What did you see? And why?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the cloth bag is best for shopping. What I saw: it held 10 kilograms and didn't tear, and the plastic bag held 5. Why: cloth is strong, and we can use it again and again, so we don't need new bags. Any honest answer with all three parts is good.
flow.think: Which bag in your home has been used the most times? Can you count?

experiments.context: This is the bag test. You add 1-kilogram weights, such as full 1-litre water bottles, one at a time to four different bags and lift them, to see which carries the most before it tears.

activities.title: Dustbin Detective: one day's waste

materials.item: a tally sheet with four columns, stuck next to the kitchen dustbin
a pencil tied to the sheet with string

schedule.what: Stick up the tally sheet in the morning. Everyone makes a mark all day. In the evening, count the marks and draw a bar chart.

activities.record: Count the marks in each column. Draw a bar chart with four bars. Circle the column you could make smaller.

flow.do: 1. Draw four columns on a sheet. Call them ROTS, KABADIWALA, COULD BE REUSED and NOTHING ELSE. Peels go under ROTS. Paper, bottles and cans go under KABADIWALA. Jars, boxes and old clothes go under COULD BE REUSED. Wrappers and packets go under NOTHING ELSE. 2. Stick it beside the dustbin. 3. Tell the whole family to make one mark for each thing they throw out today.
flow.say: Today we are waste detectives. Every time anyone throws something out, they make a mark. Tonight we'll see what our home throws out.
flow.kid: Make a sheet with four columns. Stick it by the dustbin. Each time someone throws something out, make a mark.
flow.context: This is the first step of Dustbin Detective. For one day, your family makes a mark every time something is thrown out, to see what kinds of waste your home makes.

flow.do: In the evening, count the marks in each column and draw a bar chart.
flow.say: Let's count. Which column has the most marks? Is that what you expected?
flow.kid: Count the marks in each column. Draw a bar for each one.
flow.parent: In many Indian homes, the ROTS column and the NOTHING ELSE column are the biggest. Peels and leftovers come from every meal. Wrappers and packets come with almost everything we buy. Any result is fine, because it is your home's own data.

flow.do: Look at the NOTHING ELSE column together and choose one thing to reduce this week.
flow.say: These things had nowhere good to go. Which one could we stop bringing home?
flow.kid: Look at the NOTHING ELSE column. Choose one thing your family could stop buying. Write it on the fridge.
flow.think: Where do the NOTHING ELSE things go when the garbage van takes them?

activities.context: This is a one-day survey of your home's waste. You make a tally mark each time something is thrown out, then count and compare.

activities.title: Follow the Bottle (act it out)

materials.item: an empty plastic bottle
12 sheets of paper for station signs (7 for Road 1, 5 for Road 2)

schedule.what: Put signs around the home. Carry a bottle along two journeys and act out what happens at each place.

activities.record: Draw the two journeys as two roads. Mark where the bottle ends up on each.

flow.do: Put up signs in different rooms. Road 1: SHOP, HOME, DRY WASTE BAG, WASTE PICKER OR KABADIWALA, SCRAP DEALER, FACTORY, T-SHIRT. Road 2: MIXED BAG, DUMPING GROUND, DRAIN, RIVER, SEA.
flow.say: This bottle is going on a journey. There are two roads it can take. Let's walk both.
flow.kid: Put up the signs around the house. You are going to carry this bottle on two journeys.
flow.context: This is the first step of Follow the Bottle, where you act out the two roads a plastic bottle can take after you finish with it.

flow.do: Walk Road 1 with the bottle. At each sign, your child says what happens there.
flow.say: At each place, tell me what happens to the bottle.
flow.kid: Walk Road 1. At each sign, say what happens. At the factory, pretend to shred it. Then spin it into thread.
flow.parent: Good answers. The waste picker or kabadiwala collects it and sells it to a scrap dealer. The dealer sorts thousands of bottles by kind and colour. The factory washes and shreds them into flakes, melts them and spins them into polyester fibre. The fibre becomes T-shirts, carpets or pillow filling. Most T-shirts like that are hard to recycle again.

flow.do: Walk Road 2 with the bottle. At the end, ask how long it will stay in the sea.
flow.say: Now the bottle went into a mixed bag. Where does it go?
flow.kid: Walk Road 2. Where does the bottle end up? What happens to it in the sea?
flow.parent: On Road 2, the bottle sits in a dump, or washes from a drain into a river and the sea. Sunlight cracks it into microplastics, which fish and birds swallow. Nobody knows exactly how long it lasts. Estimates are hundreds of years.
flow.think: What small thing at home decides which road the bottle takes?

activities.context: This is an act-it-out game. You carry an empty bottle around the home, past signs, to follow the two roads it can take: to a factory, or to the sea.

activities.title: Meet the Kabadiwala

materials.item: a bundle of old newspapers or bottles to sell
a notebook and pencil with five questions written in it

activities.safety: Always go with a grown-up. Be polite, and ask before taking any photos.

schedule.what: Sell some old newspapers or bottles to a kabadiwala or a scrap shop, and ask five questions.

activities.record: Write the kabadiwala's price list in your notebook. Write one thing you learned that surprised you.

flow.do: 1. Write five questions in the notebook. 2. Collect a bundle of old newspapers or rinsed bottles to sell.
flow.say: The kabadiwala is an expert on waste. Let's ask questions, like reporters.
flow.kid: Write five questions for the kabadiwala. For example: What do you buy? What don't you buy? Where does it go?
flow.context: This is the first step of Meet the Kabadiwala. You visit a person who buys old paper, metal and bottles, and find out where they go next.

flow.do: Visit the kabadiwala or a scrap shop, or wait for the one who comes to your lane. Sell the bundle. Watch it being weighed. Ask the questions.
flow.say: Please may we ask you some questions about your work?
flow.kid: Watch the bundle being weighed. Ask your questions. Write down what each thing is worth.
flow.parent: Good questions: What do you buy, and for how much per kilo? What will you not buy, and why? Where do you take it? Who taught you to tell the plastics apart? Usually newspaper, cardboard, metal, glass bottles and hard plastic sell. Chips packets, thin wrappers and dirty things don't. Prices change often, so write down what yours says.

flow.do: At home, talk about what you learned.
flow.say: What surprised you? What could we sort better at home now?
flow.kid: What surprised you? What will you sort better now?
flow.think: The kabadiwala won't buy chips packets. What happens to them instead?

activities.context: This is a visit to a kabadiwala, a person who buys old newspapers, metal and bottles from homes. You sell a bundle, and ask where it goes next.

activities.title: No-Sew T-shirt Bag

materials.item: an old cotton T-shirt that nobody wears
a pair of sharp scissors
a ruler and a pen

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts thick parts with the sharp scissors. Children can cut the fringe with help, keeping fingers away from the blades.

schedule.what: Cut off the sleeves and neck, cut a fringe along the bottom and tie it into a strong bag.

activities.record: Draw your bag. Write what it was before, and one thing you will carry in it.

flow.do: 1. Lay the T-shirt flat. 2. Cut off both sleeves, just inside the seams. 3. Cut a big scoop around the neck, about 10 cm deep. The shoulders become the handles.
flow.say: This T-shirt is too small for anyone. We're going to upcycle it, which means turning it into something more useful.
flow.kid: Lay the T-shirt flat. A grown-up cuts off the sleeves. Then they cut a big scoop at the neck.
flow.context: This is the first step of the No-Sew T-shirt Bag. You turn an old T-shirt into a strong bag without any sewing.

flow.do: 1. Turn the T-shirt inside out. 2. Along the bottom, cut strips about 8 cm long and 2 cm wide, through both layers, all the way across.
flow.say: These strips will become knots that close the bottom of the bag.
flow.kid: Turn the shirt inside out. Cut strips along the bottom, through both layers. Make them about as long as your finger.

flow.do: 1. Tie each front strip to the back strip under it, with a double knot. 2. Then tie a strip from each knot to a strip from the knot beside it, to close the gaps. 3. Turn the bag right side out.
flow.say: Tie them tight, two knots each. Then tie neighbours together, so nothing can fall through.
flow.kid: Tie each front strip to the back strip under it. Two knots. Then tie neighbours together. Turn the bag right way out.

flow.do: Test the bag with a few things from the kitchen. Use it for the bag test.
flow.say: Let's try it. Would you take this to the vegetable market?
flow.kid: Put some things in your bag. Is it strong? Keep it for the bag test.

check.q: Turning an old T-shirt into a shopping bag is called…
check.why: Upcycling means making waste into something more useful. Picking 'recycling' is close, but recycling breaks a thing down into its material first, like melting or pulping. Here the cloth is used as it is.

activities.context: This is a making activity. You turn an old T-shirt into a strong shopping bag, with scissors and knots and no sewing.

activities.title: Fold a Newspaper Bag

materials.item: a large double sheet of newspaper
flour paste (2 spoons of atta stirred into 3 spoons of water) or tape
a strip of thick paper or old card for the handle

schedule.what: Fold and paste a newspaper bag. Let the paste dry for 30 minutes (no waiting if you use tape). Use it for the bag test.

activities.record: Draw the folding steps in your own way, so you can make another one.

flow.do: 1. Fold the double sheet in half along its long side, so it is a long strip of four layers. 2. Bring the two short ends together so they overlap by 2 cm. 3. Paste the overlap. You now have a loop. Press it flat into a tube.
flow.say: Newspapers used to be folded into bags in shops all over India. Let's make one.
flow.kid: Fold the newspaper in half the long way. Bring the short ends together so they overlap. Paste them. Press it flat into a tube.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fold a Newspaper Bag. You make a paper bag from one sheet of newspaper and flour paste.

flow.do: 1. Fold up the bottom of the tube about 6 cm. 2. Open that fold into a flat diamond shape. 3. Fold the top point of the diamond down to the middle, and the bottom point up to the middle, overlapping. 4. Paste them down firmly.
flow.say: This is the tricky part. Go slowly. If it goes wrong, unfold and try again.
flow.kid: Fold the bottom up. Open it into a diamond. Fold the top and bottom points to the middle. Paste them down.
flow.parent: This bottom fold is the hard part. It usually works on the second or third try. If it won't work, simply fold the bottom up twice and paste it flat. The bag will be weaker, but still useful.

flow.do: 1. Paste the two ends of a strip of thick paper inside the top edge, on opposite sides, to make a handle loop. 2. Let the bag dry for 30 minutes. 3. Gently open it out.
flow.say: Now let it dry. Then we'll see how much it can carry.
flow.kid: Paste the ends of the handle strip inside the top. Let it dry. Then open it gently.
flow.wait: Let it dry for 30 minutes if you used paste. With tape, you can open it at once.

activities.context: This is a making activity. You fold one sheet of old newspaper into a bag, held with flour paste, the way many Indian shops once did.

activities.title: Microbe Scissors: why peels rot and plastic doesn't (a model)

materials.item: 20 paper strips, each about 2 cm wide and 15 cm long
small pieces of tape and a pen
a stapler

schedule.what: Make a 'peel chain' and a 'plastic chain' of paper rings. Be a microbe and try to take them apart.

activities.record: Draw both chains, and draw which one you could take apart.

flow.do: 1. Make a chain of 10 linked paper rings. Close each ring with a small piece of tape, and draw a dot on each tape. This is the peel chain. 2. Make a second chain of 10 rings, closed with staples. This is the plastic chain.
flow.say: Peels and plastic are both made of long chain molecules. These paper chains are giant models of them. The taped joins with a dot are places where a microbe's tool fits.
flow.kid: Make a chain of 10 rings closed with tape. Draw a dot on each tape. Make another chain closed with staples.
flow.context: This is the first step of Microbe Scissors, a model of why peels rot and plastic does not. Paper chains stand in for long molecules.

flow.do: 1. Your child is a microbe. 2. Rule: a microbe can only open a ring where there is a dot. 3. Give one minute to take each chain apart into single rings.
flow.say: You're a microbe. Your enzymes only fit where there is a dot. You have one minute for each chain. Go!
flow.kid: You are a microbe. You can only open rings with a dot. Take each chain apart. One minute each. Go!

check.q: In the Microbe Scissors model, the microbe could open the peel chain but not the plastic chain. What do the dots stand for?
options: Places where the microbe's enzymes fit the molecule
check.why: Each enzyme fits only certain joins in a molecule, like a key fits a lock. Peel molecules have joins that soil enzymes fit. Most plastics have none. Picking 'where the sun shines' mixes up rotting with sunlight cracking, which is the next step of the model.

flow.do: 1. Now the parent is the Sun. Tear the plastic chain into pieces of two or three rings. 2. Then draw a dot on just two plastic rings, and let the microbe try again, slowly.
flow.say: The Sun cracks plastic into smaller pieces. But are they gone? No. They are still plastic chains, only shorter. Those are microplastics. Now, in 2016 scientists found a real microbe with a key for one kind of plastic. Let's add two dots.
flow.kid: The Sun breaks the plastic chain into small bits. Are they gone? Now two rings get dots. Can the microbe open them?
flow.parent: This shows three real ideas. Microbes rot what their enzymes fit. Sunlight only breaks plastic into smaller plastic. And a few microbes, like Ideonella sakaiensis, found in Japan in 2016, have begun to evolve enzymes for one plastic, slowly.
flow.think: Why do you think the plastic-eating microbe was found near a bottle recycling plant?

activities.context: This is a model. Two paper chains stand for a peel molecule and a plastic molecule. You pretend to be a microbe that can only cut certain joins.

activities.title: Repair Day

materials.item: one broken thing: a shirt with a missing button, a torn book page, a sock with a small hole or a toy that has come apart
a needle, thread and a spare button, or tape, or glue, depending on the repair

activities.safety: A grown-up threads the needle and watches the sewing. Use glue only with a grown-up.

schedule.what: Mend one broken thing at home. Then watch a repair person at work, if one is near.

activities.record: Draw the thing before and after. Write how long the repair took, and how long the thing may now last.

flow.do: Hunt around the home for one broken thing that could be mended.
flow.say: Let's find something that's broken but not finished. What could we mend?
flow.kid: Find one broken thing at home. A shirt with no button? A torn book? A toy in pieces?
flow.context: This is the first step of Repair Day. You mend one broken thing at home, the way repairers in every Indian street do.

flow.do: Mend it together. For a button, knot the thread. Push the needle up through one hole and down through the next. Do this six times, then knot it underneath. For a book: tape the tear on both sides. For a sock: sew small stitches across the hole, back and forth.
flow.say: Slow and careful. Repairers are patient people.
flow.kid: Mend your thing with a grown-up. Small careful stitches, or neat tape. Take your time.
flow.parent: A button usually takes a child about 10 to 15 minutes the first time. That is fine. Darning a big hole is hard, so choose a small one.

flow.do: If you can, visit a cobbler, a tailor or a cycle puncture shop. Ask if you can watch for a few minutes.
flow.say: Let's watch an expert. What tools do they use?
flow.kid: Watch a repair person. What tools do they use? What are they mending?
flow.parent: At a puncture shop, watch the tube being pushed into a tub of water. Bubbles show where the hole is. If no repair shop is near, skip this step, or ask an older relative or neighbour to show something they used to mend.

check.q: Why is repairing a chappal usually better for the planet than buying a new one?
options: A new chappal would need new rubber, a factory, a truck and packaging
check.why: Making anything uses up materials and energy. A repair uses a little thread and someone's skill. Picking 'no difference' means thinking only of the old chappal, not of everything a new one would use.

projects.title: Handmade Recycled Paper, and a Thank-you Card

materials.item: used paper: newspaper, old notebook pages or egg trays (not shiny magazine paper)
a bucket or big bowl of water, and a wide tub
a mixer, used by a grown-up, or a whisk or your hands
an old photo frame with a piece of mosquito net taped tightly over it, or a steel tea strainer
2 old cotton cloths or towels, and a rolling pin

projects.safety: Only a grown-up uses the mixer. Never put hands into the mixer jar.

schedule.what: Tear the used paper into stamp-sized pieces. Soak them in water overnight.
Make the pulp. Lift sheets on the net frame. Press them on cloth with a rolling pin. Leave them to dry.
Check if the sheets are dry. If they are still damp, leave them another day.
Peel off the dry sheets. Compare them with the old paper. Make a thank-you card for the person who collects your waste.

projects.record: Stick a small piece of your recycled paper beside a piece of newspaper in your notebook. Write three ways they are different.

flow.do: 1. Tear about four double sheets of newspaper into pieces the size of a stamp. 2. Put them in a bucket and cover with water. 3. Leave overnight.
flow.say: We're going to do what a paper recycling factory does, in our kitchen. First the paper has to soak, so its fibres loosen.
flow.kid: Tear the paper into tiny pieces. Put them in water. Leave them overnight.
flow.wait: Leave the paper to soak overnight.
flow.context: This is the first step of the recycled paper project. You soak, mash and press old paper into new sheets, then make a card.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up puts two handfuls of soaked paper and lots of water into the mixer. 2. Blend in short bursts until it looks like thin grey porridge. 3. Pour it into the wide tub and add water until it is about one part pulp to three parts water.
flow.say: Look at the pulp. Those tiny threads are wood fibres, from trees cut years ago.
flow.kid: A grown-up blends the wet paper into grey mush. Look closely. Can you see tiny threads?
flow.parent: No mixer? Squeeze and rub the soaked paper between your hands for 10 minutes, or beat it with a whisk. The paper will be rougher, but it works.

flow.do: 1. Stir the tub. 2. Slide the net frame into the tub, under the pulp. 3. Lift it out flat and slowly, so a thin even layer sits on the net. 4. Let it drip. 5. Turn it face down onto a cloth and lift the frame off. 6. Cover with a second cloth and roll firmly with the rolling pin.
flow.say: Lift slowly and keep it flat. A thin, even layer makes good paper.
flow.kid: Slide the frame under the mush. Lift it out flat. Let it drip. Flip it onto a cloth. Roll it flat.
flow.parent: If the layer is too thin, it will tear. Dip again and add more pulp. If it sticks to the net, press the back of the net with a sponge before lifting. A tea strainer makes small round sheets, which are perfect for cards.

flow.do: Leave the sheets on their cloth in a shady, airy place. Check the next day.
flow.say: Now the water has to leave. Where will it go?
flow.kid: Leave your sheets to dry. Check them tomorrow. Are they dry all the way through?
flow.wait: Leave the sheets to dry for 1 to 2 days. In the monsoon it can take 3 days.
flow.parent: Drying in shade keeps the sheets flat. In strong sun they dry faster, but may curl.

flow.do: 1. Peel the dry sheet gently off the cloth. 2. Compare it with newspaper. 3. Make a thank-you card for the person who collects your waste, and give it.
flow.say: Look what our old newspaper became. Who should get our first card?
flow.kid: Peel off your new paper. How does it feel? Make a thank-you card for the person who takes your waste. Give it to them.

check.q: Your recycled paper is rougher and thicker than the newspaper it came from. Why?

Water made it heavier for ever
It is made of plastic now

quiz.p: Which of these comes first, and saves the most?
quiz.why: Reducing means the waste is never made, so nothing has to be collected, melted or dumped. Picking 'recycle' is the most common answer, because recycling is talked about most. But it still uses energy and trucks.

quiz.p: Arjun, a boy in Class 3, finds that his school shirt has lost a button. What is the best thing to do?
quiz.why: Sewing on a button takes minutes, and the shirt keeps working for years. Picking 'recycle' skips a step: mending comes before breaking a thing down.

quiz.p: In the rot jar test, why do we watch the jars for two whole weeks, and not just for one day?
opts: Rotting is slow, so one day would show almost no change
The jars need two weeks to get warm
Plastic needs two weeks to rot
quiz.why: Microbes take days to grow on the peel and cut it apart. After one day, every jar would look the same, and we could not tell what rots. Two weeks is long enough to see a clear difference.
quiz.context: In the rot jar test, you bury a banana peel, newspaper, cotton cloth and a strip of milk packet in damp soil in clear jars, and watch for two weeks.

quiz.p: Look at the made-up jar results. Which thing was left almost unchanged?
quiz.why: The milk packet scored 5, meaning all of it was left. Picking the cloth is a fair second guess, because cotton rots slowly. But it does rot, and plastic does not.
quiz.context: In the rot jar test, you bury a banana peel, newspaper, cotton cloth and a strip of milk packet in damp soil in clear jars, and watch for two weeks.

chart.title: Made-up results: how much was left on day 14 (5 means all of it, 0 means none)

quiz.p: Why does a banana peel rot in soil?
opts: Microbes feed on it, using enzymes that cut its molecules
quiz.why: Bacteria and fungi pour out enzymes that cut the peel's long molecules into food. Picking 'rain washes it away' means thinking the peel just moves. In a covered jar it still rots, so living things must be doing it.

quiz.p: A wooden spoon and a plastic spoon are buried side by side in damp soil. After a year, the wooden spoon is soft and crumbling, but the plastic spoon looks the same. Why?
opts: Soil microbes have enzymes that fit wood, but almost none that fit plastic
The plastic spoon was buried deeper
quiz.why: Microbes have fed on wood for millions of years, so they have enzymes that fit it. Plastic is new, and almost no microbe has an enzyme for plastic. Both spoons were in the same soil, so the material made the difference.

quiz.p: A girl bakes a tray of damp soil in a hot oven, so that every microbe in the soil dies. When it cools, she buries a banana peel in it and seals the jar. What will happen to the peel?
opts: It will hardly rot, because there are no microbes to feed on it
It will rot faster, because the soil is warm
It will rot just as fast as in garden soil
quiz.why: Rotting is microbes feeding. With no microbes, the peel stays almost whole for a long time. Picking 'just as fast' means thinking the soil itself does the rotting. This is how people keep food from rotting: heating and sealing it, as in a jar of pickle or a sealed tin.

quiz.p: Why should a family keep wet waste and dry waste in separate bins?
opts: So the wet waste can be composted and the dry waste stays clean enough to recycle
quiz.why: Peels in their own bin can go to compost. Paper, metal and plastic kept dry and clean can be sold to the kabadiwala. Mixed together, both are spoilt, and most of it goes to the dump.

quiz.p: What does a kabadiwala do with the old newspapers they buy from homes?
opts: Sells them on to dealers, who send them to paper mills to be made into new paper
quiz.why: Kabadiwalas buy, weigh and sort old paper, metal and bottles, then sell them on. That is how a lot of India's waste paper gets back to the mills.

quiz.p: Which of these places turns vegetable peels into something useful?
opts: A compost yard, where microbes turn them into compost for plants
quiz.why: In a compost yard, peels rot with air and become dark, crumbly compost that feeds plants. In a dump they rot without air and make methane gas. In a river they make the water dirty.

quiz.p: Riya, a girl in Class 3, cuts up an old T-shirt and ties it into a shopping bag. What is this called?
quiz.why: Upcycling makes waste into something more useful. Downcycling makes it into something of lower quality.

quiz.p: In the bag test, why do we lift every bag the same height and hold it for 10 seconds?
opts: So the test is fair: only the bag is different
quiz.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If every bag is lifted the same way, any difference in what they hold comes from the bags. Picking 'gets tired' treats a bag like a person.
quiz.context: In the bag test, you add 1-kilogram weights to a bag one at a time, and count how many kilograms it holds before it tears.

quiz.p: In 2016, scientists found a bacterium that eats PET bottle plastic. What do most scientists say about this bacterium?
opts: They have already cleaned up the oceans
They are real and exciting, but slow, and work mainly on one kind of plastic
quiz.why: Ideonella sakaiensis is real, but they took weeks to eat a thin film, and only PET. Scientists are still debating how much such microbes can help. Picking 'cleaned up the oceans' trusts a hopeful headline more than the evidence.

quiz.p: Scientists still argue about which of these?
opts: Whether recycling alone can solve the plastic problem, or whether we must make much less plastic
Whether plastic is made by people
quiz.why: Everyone agrees that plastic is made by people and that peels rot. Some scientists say better recycling is the answer. Others say so little plastic is recycled that the only real answer is to make much less of it.

quiz.p: Only about how many out of every 100 parts of all plastic waste ever made have been recycled, by a 2017 estimate?
quiz.why: Roland Geyer, Jenna Jambeck and Kara Lavender Law estimated about 9 out of 100. About 79 out of 100 are in dumps or loose in nature. Picking 'about 50' or more is common, because recycling bins make it feel as if most plastic is recycled.

applications: Compost pits and biogas plants turn wet waste into soil food and cooking gas.
Kabadiwalas, scrap dealers and waste pickers run one of the biggest recycling systems in the world.
Old PET bottles are spun into polyester fibre for pillows, carpets, jackets and even school uniforms.
Steel and aluminium from old cars, cans and utensils are melted down and remade.
Old newspapers and cardboard are pulped into egg trays, new boxes and paper bags.
Broken glass is melted into new bottles and jars.
Shredded plastic has been mixed into tar to build roads in India. Professor Rajagopalan Vasudevan in Madurai helped develop this.
Engineers are testing plastic-eating enzymes to turn old bottles back into the building blocks of new plastic.
Old saris become kantha quilts, rugs and bags, and rag-weavers make durries from cloth scraps.
Repair shops fix phones, cycles, shoes, pressure cookers, umbrellas and fans on almost every Indian street.
Hospitals keep needles and medical waste separate, so they can be treated safely.
Artists build sculptures and gardens from waste, like Nek Chand's Rock Garden in Chandigarh.

open_questions.q: How long does plastic really last?
open_questions.why_open: Most plastic has existed for less than 75 years. Times like '450 years' come from speeded-up tests and are rough guesses. Different plastics, and different places, give very different answers.

open_questions.q: What do microplastics do inside animals and people?
open_questions.why_open: They have been found in fish, birds, soil animals and human bodies. Scientists are still studying whether, and how, they cause harm.

open_questions.q: Will microbes in nature evolve to eat plastic?
open_questions.why_open: A few bacteria and fungi have been found that break down some plastics slowly. Nobody knows how fast this will spread, or whether it will reach the plastics that matter most.

open_questions.q: Do wax worms truly digest plastic bags?
open_questions.why_open: Some experiments say yes, and enzymes have been found in their saliva. Other scientists question how much plastic is really broken down, rather than just chewed.

open_questions.q: Did fungi that could rot wood evolve late, and is that why coal formed?
open_questions.why_open: Gene studies and rock studies point in different directions. Both may be partly right.

open_questions.q: What is the best way for a whole country to cut its waste?
open_questions.why_open: Bans, deposits on bottles, making companies pay for their packaging and supporting waste pickers all help in some places. Experts still argue about which works best, and for whom.

open_questions.q: How much of India's waste do waste pickers really recycle?
open_questions.why_open: Most of their work is not counted by any office. Estimates differ a lot.

maths.problem: In the bag test, the newspaper bag held 2 kilograms. The cloth bag held 10 kilograms. How many times as much did the cloth bag hold?
maths.explain: The cloth bag held 10 kilograms. The newspaper bag held 2. 10 divided by 2 is 5. You can check: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 10. So the cloth bag held 5 times as much.
maths.context: In the bag test, you put 1-kilogram weights into a bag one at a time, lift it, and count how many kilograms it holds before it tears.
maths.why_maths: Saying 'the cloth bag is stronger' is a start. Dividing tells us how much stronger: five times.

maths.problem: In the bag test, the T-shirt bag held 7 kilograms. At the market, you buy 2 kilograms of potatoes, 1 kilogram of onions, 1 kilogram of tomatoes and half a kilogram of peas. Can the T-shirt bag carry it all? How much room is left?
maths.answer: Yes. The vegetables weigh 4 and a half kilograms, so there are 2 and a half kilograms to spare.
maths.explain: Add the vegetables: 2 + 1 + 1 = 4 kilograms, and the peas make it 4 and a half. The bag held 7 kilograms. 7 take away 4 and a half is 2 and a half. So the bag can carry it all, with 2 and a half kilograms to spare.
maths.context: In the bag test, you load each bag with 1-kilogram weights, such as full 1-litre water bottles, one at a time. One litre of water weighs about 1 kilogram.
maths.why_maths: The test tells you what a bag can hold. Adding up a real shopping list tells you whether it is strong enough for your family's market trip.

maths.problem: In Dustbin Detective, a family made these marks in one day. ROTS: 12. KABADIWALA: 7. COULD BE REUSED: 3. NOTHING ELSE: 9. Draw a bar chart. Which column was biggest, and how many marks were there in all?
maths.answer: ROTS was biggest, with 12 marks. There were 31 marks in all. Here is the bar chart.
maths.explain: Draw one bar for each column, as tall as its number. The tallest bar is ROTS, at 12. To find the total, add them: 12 + 7 = 19. 19 + 3 = 22. 22 + 9 = 31.
maths.context: In Dustbin Detective, your family makes one tally mark beside the dustbin each time something is thrown out, in one of four columns.

answer_chart.title: One day's waste marks in one home (made-up)

maths.why_maths: A list of tally marks is hard to read. A bar chart shows at a glance which kind of waste your home makes most, so you know what to reduce first.

maths.problem: Scientists estimated that out of every 100 parts of plastic waste ever made, 9 were recycled and 12 were burned. How many out of 100 were neither recycled nor burned?
maths.explain: Recycled and burned together make 9 + 12 = 21. Take 21 away from 100. 100 minus 21 is 79. So 79 out of every 100 parts are in dumps or loose in nature.
maths.context: In 2017, three scientists added up all the plastic waste ever made in the world, up to 2015, and worked out what happened to it.
maths.why_maths: Scientists often give two numbers and leave the third hidden. Adding and taking away finds the hidden one, and here it is the biggest and most important.

maths.problem: A family puts out about 2 kilograms of wet waste every day. How much is that in one week? If they compost it all, how much less goes to the dump in a week?
maths.answer: 14 kilograms in a week. Composting would keep all 14 kilograms out of the dump.
maths.explain: There are 7 days in a week. 2 kilograms each day for 7 days is 7 times 2, which is 14. If all of it goes to the compost pot, 14 kilograms less goes to the dump.
maths.context: Wet waste is peels, tea leaves and leftover food. Many Indian families throw out a kilogram or two of it every day.
maths.why_maths: One day's peels look small. Multiplying shows how quickly they add up, and how much one compost pot can save.

roots.context: We have been learning where waste goes, and why some things rot and others don't. Now we ask what waste tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the same damp soil, the peel rotted and the plastic stayed the same. Soil microbes have fed on dead plants for millions of years, so they have enzymes that fit them. Plastic is new, and almost no microbe has an enzyme for plastic yet. So whether a thing rots depends on the living things around it as much as on the thing itself.
deep_truth.habit: We say a peel is 'biodegradable' and plastic is not, as if rotting were hidden inside the material. But rotting is something living things do when they feed. A material rots only once some living thing has the tools to eat it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the rot jar test, the peel went black and soft and grew white threads of fungus, while the milk packet looked new after 14 days. Long ago, wood may have piled up as coal partly because few fungi could rot it. In 2016, a bacterium was found that feeds on bottle plastic.

three.who_am_i: Your food grew in soil that microbes made from old leaves and peels. So part of you was once something that rotted.
three.what_is_life: Almost every living thing becomes food for others when they die. Microbes take them apart, and new plants grow from what is left.
three.what_is_this_world: A world where leaves, peels and bodies are taken apart and used again. Plastic is one of the few things it cannot yet take apart.

roots.thread: In a forest, a fallen leaf feeds fungi and worms. What is left becomes soil, and the soil feeds a tree. The same atoms take turns as leaf, worm, soil and tree. Plastic stays out of this circle for now, because almost nothing can take it apart.

teachings.teaching: Everything in this changing world is filled with the one Lord. Enjoy it by letting go. Do not grab, for whose is all this wealth?
teachings.link: Reducing means taking only what we need. The atoms in everything we own were part of the Earth before us, and will be after us.

teachings.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, The Heart of Understanding, 1988
teachings.teaching: Look deeply at a sheet of paper and you can see a cloud in it. Without the cloud, no rain. Without rain, no tree. Without the tree, no paper. He called this 'interbeing': nothing exists on its own.
teachings.link: Your recycled paper carries the same cloud, rain and tree, and the work of the people who collected it.

teachings.teaching: One of the five great vows of Jainism is aparigraha, not holding on to more things than we need.
teachings.link: Fewer things means less waste, and less harm to the many living beings that waste reaches.

science.text: Matter is never created or destroyed, only rearranged. Antoine and Marie-Anne Lavoisier's careful weighing in the 1780s helped show this.
Microbes have been breaking down and recycling the materials of dead living things for billions of years. Without them, the Earth would be buried in dead leaves and bodies.

other_view.view: Waste is a practical problem of materials, money and rules. Better recycling, fair pay for waste pickers and smart laws can solve it. There is no need to bring in oneness or the self. That is an honest view, and much of the work it calls for is the same.

practice.title: Look deeply at one thing
practice.say: Pick up one thing near you: a steel tumbler, a pencil or a piece of paper. Hold it in both hands. Close your eyes and breathe slowly three times. Now picture where it came from: the mine, the tree, the factory, and the hands that made and carried this thing. Breathe again. Now picture where it will go when you are finished with it. Open your eyes. Look at it as if for the first time.
practice.kid: Hold one thing in both hands. Close your eyes. Breathe slowly three times. Where did it come from? Where will it go? Open your eyes and look at it again.

ask: If one day a microbe evolves an enzyme that fits plastic, will plastic become biodegradable?
If nothing ever really goes away, what does 'throwing away' mean?
Is anything truly yours, if its atoms were here before you and will stay after you?

how_we_found_out.story: For years, shops sold plastic bags labelled 'biodegradable'. Many people believed these bags would soon rot away after they were thrown out. Imogen Napper, a young scientist at the University of Plymouth in England, decided to test the labels. With Richard Thompson, the scientist guiding her work, she took five kinds of shopping bag. One was ordinary plastic. The others were sold as biodegradable or compostable. They left pieces of each bag in three places: buried in soil, out in the open air, and under the sea. Then they checked them for three years. In the open air, sunlight crumbled every kind of bag into small pieces within a year. But in the soil and the sea, most bags were still whole. After three years, several 'biodegradable' bags could still carry a full load of shopping. The compostable bag disappeared in the sea within three months. In the soil, it was still there after more than two years, though too weak to carry shopping. Their results, published in 2019, showed that a label is a promise, not evidence. Only a test can show what really happens.
how_we_found_out.who: Imogen Napper and Richard Thompson, University of Plymouth, England
how_we_found_out.when: Published in 2019, after a three-year test
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Bags labelled 'biodegradable' rot away soon after they are thrown out. After three years in soil and in the sea, most of them were still whole, and some could still carry shopping.
